On the Orders of the Day:

I have a question to put which is of some urgency, and as the Minister of Labour is not in his seat perhaps onh of the other ministers might reply. The strike at Winnipeg seems to have developed into serious proportions, all the public services of the city being practically in a state of collapse. Is the Government in a position to say what measures have been taken to prevent the strike spreading; whether a compulsory investigation under the Industrial Disputes Act has been applied for, and if so, will it be granted?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not wish
my hon. friend to understand that the Government have not been making any efforts to end the strike. My hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) has, in every possible way, lent his services to composing the differences which have arisen. More than that, on Friday evening last, I addressed a personal appeal to the head of the Trades and Labour Council in Winnipeg. I have not a copy of it before me at the moment, but later on in the day, if I have the opportunity, I shall bring it down and make the House acquainted with its terms. It is perfectly true that the Government has not seen its way clear to act upon some of the suggestions which have been presented to us but, apart from that, every effort that could possibly be made by conciliatory methods to compose this difficulty has been made. I hope my hon. friend will realize that. Further, it is hoped that, to-day or tormorrow, some more effective effort can be undertaken.

7.	Is the statement in the Toronto Saturday Night, of date May 18, 1918, that "Dr. R. J. McFall has been loaned to the Food Control Organization to continue the work originated by Mr. O'Connor," correct?
8.	Has any Order in Council been passed appointing Dr. R. J. McFall to perform in the same manner under the same circumstances, and under the same conditions the work which Mr. O'Connor previous to his resignation performed for the Minister of Labour? If not. how has the appointment of Dr. McFall been made, if made, and under what authority?
9.	What salary and living allowance, or either, will the new appointee receive, and out of what fund and through what department of Government or under what Commission will he act?

11.	Will the new appointee act under direction of the Minister of Labour alone, and if not, under what other arrangement?

13.	Does the Government intend to merge any, and what, of the operations previously con-

ducted by Mr. O'Connor with the same or similar operations of the Canada Pood Board or of any other Board or Department of Government, and if so, for what reason?

speechtext: On motion of Hon. A. K. Maclean, Bill No. 84, to amend the Business Profits War Tax Act, 1916, was read the third time and passed.
Hon. A. K. MACLEAN moved the third reading of Bill No. 85, to amend The Income War Tax Act, 1917.

Many business men and others affected by the Income Tax Act of last year experienced some difficulty in preparing the return which they were required to furnish to the Government. Some weeks ago I handed to Mr. Boville, Deputy Minister of Finance, a primer prepared by the Treasury Department in the United States, which furnishes all information arising out of the administration and application of their Income Tax Act. Quite unwittingly, many people have made errors in their returns, and if the department-would prepare a primer similar to that sent out by the United States Treasury Department, those affected by the Act would be considerably assisted in the preparation of returns. Mr. Boville was struck with the necessity of such an official publication, the cost of which would not be very large. Last year some of the financial and trust companies and banks prepared publications of this kind for the benefit of their own ' patrons. I saw three or four of them, but they did not appear to be very complete. I think it would be good policy on the part of the department to-have such a primer issued during the present fiscal year.
I think that a publication of that nature is now in course of preparation. At any rate, my hon. friend's suggestion is a very timely one, and I shall convey it to the Minister of Finance.

I suggest that the department issue also a table showing
the amounts paid under different incomes according to the new provisions.
That is, for circulation outside of the House?
Yes.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the third time and passed.

On motion of Hon. T. A. Crerar, Minister of Agriculture, Bill No. 108, to amend the Inspection and -Sale Act (Fruit, fruit marks and potatoes), was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-definitions:
Has this Bill been distributed? I do not have it on my file.
It has been printed.
Is this part of the amendments that have been brought up by the Minister of Trade and Commerce as regards the Inspection and Sale Act?
No.
This is new legislation?
Entirely.
Who is the minister who has charge of this legislation?

Part IX of the Inspection and Sale Act, relating to fruit, fruit marks and fruit packages, is under the jurisdiction of the Department of Agriculture, and these amendments refer only to that particular portion of the Act. They do not relate to the other matters that the Minister of Trade and Commerce submitted to the House.

I do not know how long this Bill has been printed, but it has not yet come to my notice. I have often heard the remark thrown across the floor of this House: Such and such legislation was submitted to the House and was concurred in by you. Why did you not raise an objection when it was brought before the House? The first reading of this Bill took place on the 18th of May, (that is Saturday last), and as we are supposed to observe Sunday, very little time has been given to us to look into the matter. I do not know anything aibout the importance of the legislation. I do not know whether it affects fruit growing, or fruit classification, or the marking of fruit, or the preservation of fruit. I am not an expert in regard to these matters,

but I should like to have an opportunity of looking into the Bill. It is only fair that hon. members should have an opportunity of doing so, unless the minister, makes a statement, giving us the details, and telling us what precautions have been taken to justify hon. members in letting the Bill go through without any further investigation on their part.
Legislation of this kind has been under consideration for two or three years.
How long has this Bill been submitted to the House for consideration?
The resolution has been on the Order Paper since the first of May.
When was the Bill distributed?

I do not know when it was distributed. I have had a printed copy for a considerable length of time. During the winter there was held here a convention of representative fruit growers, some consumers, and also dealers in fruit. The result of the work of that convention is embodied in this Bill.
Where do the people come in?

The consumers were represented at the convention. In respect to section 319, the only important change is that which relates to the definition of the word "culls." In the section as it previously stood, the definition of "culls" was as follows:
"Culls" shall include fruit that is either very small for the variety or immature, or the skin of which is broken so as to expose the tissue beneath, or that is so injured by insects, fungi, abnormal growths, or other causes, as' to render it unmerchantable.
The difficulty was this, that, no matter how scabby or deformed fruit was, it could not be classed as unmerchantable, and consequently there was a very wide range in the character of fruit that was classed as "culls." The amendment seeks to make that more specific, and provides, in later sections, for closer definitions of the grades. This is the section as amended:
(c) "culls" means fruit that is either very small for the variety, is seriously deformed, or has fifteen per cent or more of its surface affected by any of or by the combined injuries caused by apple scaib (Venturis, pomi), insects, cuts, bruises or other causes, or the flesh of which is not in an edible condition, or the skin of which is broken so as to expose the tissue beneath.
['Mr. Bureau.]
It will thus be apparent that the purport of the amendment is more clearly to define what is a cull in the designation of this particular class of fruit.

Does the word " bruises " covet a case where the flesh would 'be partially uneatable, but where the fruit would otherwise be good? Sometimes
12 noon you see part of a pear, say at the bottom end, if it has been standing, as big as a twenty-five cent piece or a fifty cent piece, uneatable, although the rest of the pear is perfectly good. The section states that the whole of the flesh should be uneatable. Would a case like the one I have cited by covered by the word " bruises?"
I should think it would.

The Minister of Agriculture is deserving of every credit for bringing forward this legislation. The matters pertaining to this Bill have been under consideration by Ministers of Agriculture for some years past. Within the last few months there were brought here from different provinces representatives who were in touch with fruit conditions in those provinces; consumers were also brought here,- and this Bill was framed under the supervision of all those parties.

What consumers
were brought here?

I understand from the Department of. Agriculture that representative consumers from different parts of the country were consulted in regard to this measure. Moreover, this legislation is in the public interest. Nova Scotia fruit growers, for instance, were unable to sell their -apples in the United States owing to the standard size of their barrels not conforming with the regulations enforced in the United States-. The standard barrel will be the same throughout the Dominion of Canada. The sizes of the different packages the same-. In our western provinces over one thousand cars of apples put up in packages were disposed of last year at various prices.
The goods have to be packed in containers of uniform -size, and in this way not only is the consumer protected, but the producer benefits from being able to sell his goods as up to a certain- standard. With regard to peaches, plums, pears and other fruits, the baskets in which they are to be sold are *standardized, and the consumer is protected, whereas in days gone by ail kinds of packages have been sold at different

prices, and. it is the consumer that has heen fleeced at every turn.

I did not "wish to he understood as, objecting to the Bill, and the very fact that I said I knew nothing about fruit growing should have convinced any one I was not taking exception to it. What I was objecting to was that we have not had time to look into the Bill, and I wanted to make inquiries and hear from those who understood this business before forming an opinion. I am perfectly in accord with the purpose of the Bill, but if I were a little wickeder I would say that the manner of bringing the Bill before the House .looks like an attempt to railroad it through.

I see that all packages not branded according to the Act shall be forfeited. I think this would toe unfair to the small dealers. For instance, a farmer who sells to his neighbour might toe liable to a penalty under the law.

I do not think there need toe any misapprehension on that point. It is a simple matter for the grower of fruit to stamp his name on the container. As I understand it, the small growers of fruit bring theiT produce to the market, where it is bought by dealers and shipped, perhaps to other parts of the country. It is a simple matter to put one's name on, a box toy means of a rubber stamp, and I would repeat, this legislation has been asked for by the fruit growers themselves more insistently than by any other class.
Suppose a farmer with a small orchard of fifty trees and twenty (barrels of apples, disposes of his fruit to a /consumer at home. Has he to go to the trouble of branding the barrels?

I am of the opinion the
Act would not apply in the case of one farmer selling to another Tight across the road.
Or to a man in town?

Not if he was selling
direct to the consumer. I think the law would be reasonably interpreted in cases of that kind. The Bill is designed to cover more particularly the export of fruit from one district to anotheT district.
I do not think the Bill is very plain on that point, and it may cause a great deal of inconvenience to the farmer and loss to the consumer also.

The definition of fruit is: "Fruit shall not include wild fruit, nor
cranberries, whether wild or cultivated." Why is wild fruit excluded?
I do not know the precise reason why wild fruit was excluded* but I take it that it is because very little wild fruit is sold.
Quite the contrary. Lots of raspberries, blackberries, blueberries and other kinds of wild fruits are traded in very extensively in Ontario.
The main provisions of the Bill aim at correcting the abuses that have existed in the past in connection with the sale of apples, pears and the larger varieties of fruit.
But the Bill does not cover retail transactions. That was the point I raised a moment ago.
I should like to have the minister's definition of tomatoes. Are they a fruit or a vegetable?

The question is rather
a poser, but I would call a tomato a vegetable rather than a fruit.

Webster's dictionary defines fruit thus:
Whatever is produced for the enjoyment of man or animals by the processes of vegetable growth ; that part of plants, which contains the seed.
Tomatoes contain the seed, and therefore I contend they are a fruit, and not a vegetable, according to this definition.
What about a pumpkin?
And cucumbers?

I think the definition of "immature fruit" is so vague that it may cause no end of trouble to the department in administering the Act. The definition reads:
"Immature fruit" means fruit not ripe enough for dessert purposes and which will not attain such condition after being picked from the tree, hush, plant or vine.
Now what are dessert purposes for one may not be dessert purposes for another. 1 presume that what the minister had in mind in framing this section was fruit so immature as to be unhealthy for consumption, and I would suggest the advisability of describing immature fruit as fruit unfit for human consumption or something of that sort, and then if the /question arose :n the application of the Act the testimony of a medical man could be given as to the fruit's fitness for human consumption. Bud as it is, one housewife might condemn a

certain fruit for dessert purposes which another housewife would put on her table for dessert. I think the present definition is altogether too vague.
We shall have to standardize tastes.
That might be a very difficult matter.

We should get ourselves into a hopeless tangle if we endeavoured to get the consumers to agree on a definition of immature fruit. Immature fruit means fruit that will not attain, after packing, that perfection of ripeness that will permit it to be used for dessert purposes. I am not an expert .in fruit, but I put the very question that my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMiaster) raises to the officials of my department, who, I believe, are very good officials, and who have a thorough knowledge of the business, and they gave the reasons I have , just given here. Fruit may be picked before it is entirely ripe and will attain a mature condition after it has been picked. Such fruit as that is covered by this section. On the other hand, you could pick fruit that might'be half green and that would under no condition attain maturity. This is the definition that fruit dealers who have studied the problem have made, and it is proposed as a means of preventing the sale of immature fruit.

I do not doubt the ability of the officials in the hon. gentleman's department .to judge as to the different qualities of fruit, but whether they are qualified to give a considered opinion as to the effect of a statute is quite another matter. I wouldi suggest to my hon. friend that if he substituted for the words, " for dessert purposes," the words " to be eaten raw without danger to health," he would be setting up a standard or criterion which would be possible of establishment. If it should be made to read:
"Immature fruit" means fruit not ripe enough to be eaten raw without danger to health and which will hot attain such condition after being picked from the tree, bush, plant or vine.
it would better serve the purpose.

If the minister agrees to that we will he getting into a worse muddle than ever. What is one man's meat may be another man's poison. I know lots oc people who like to eat fruit on the raw side, which would be considered unfit by others.
I do not see any better form than that in which the minister has put it. Let everybody judge for himself.
EMr. McMaster.]

The object of this clause is to put >a stop to the sale of immature fruit on the market, such as plums and other fruit brought in possibly from the United States at an early period, which is certainly immature and not fit for consumption. Without some such provision as this, fruit of that description could be brought in.

Would my hon. friend
from East Lambton (Mr. Arm-strong) tell us if this description " fruit not ripe enough for dessert purposes" applies to cooked or raw fruit? Somebody might' buy fruit to make preserves or with the idea of using it after cooking. The question o-f quality, or standard of maturity, would depend on whether the fruit was to he eaten cooked or in its natural condition. I think that if we were to put in the words " for home consumption, whether cooked or otherwise," that would cover the case.

The word " dessert " does not quite convey the idea that the minister attributes to it. Fruit, in its natural state, is uncooked. Sometimes it is called green." Green fruit is ripe fruit in the opinion of -some people. If you were to use the words " fruit in its natural state " I think it would better meet the case. The word " dessert " is usually applied to fruit which follows dinner, whereas, this should apply to the fruit that you eat as a first course at breakfast. You would not call it [DOT]" dessert " fruit if you used it in this way. It surely is intended to apply to fruit that you can eat without any bad effect upon the stomach. I would suggest to the minister that the words " fruit in its natural state " should be adopted because that will cover fruit whether it .is green or cooked.
I would like to hear from our learned, scientific men who have the health of the people in their keeping and who look after all hygenic conditions.

I think the clause is all right. "Dessert" means ordinary fruit served after -a meal1 in its raw, unprepared or uncooked state. I think that the gentlemen in the department who drew the clause -drew it with a knowledge of what they were doing and with that interpretation in view. We do not ordinarily partake of dessert fruit in a cooked condition. This is r-aw fruit and cooked fruit is prepared or preserved fruit. It is preserved by boiling and under ordinary conditions it could

not be served otherwise. In the cooking process you reduce the immature acids in the green, or partially ripe fruit, to an innocuous condition. When you take up the question as to whether it is unripe or not you open the door to enormous degrees of difference as between ripeness and unripeness. People could pick up the windfalls in the orchard or under the plum trees and sell them as fruit. I think the proper definition has been selected by those who understand the conditions and it is used to describe fruit abundantly ripened and as it is ordinarily served after a meal for dessert purposes.

I do not think it can mean that. It might be applied to fruit offered for sale for cooking. If my hon. friend (Mr. Sheard) believes that after the fruit is cooked all danger from eating it is gone, I suppose we must accept his opinion on that subject.

The clause gives a classification to immature fruit, and consequently it is all right. The difficulty in shipping fruit a distance has been that there is a temptation to pull the fruit before it is sufficiently mature. After it is picked it will develop such a degree of flavour and maturity as will indicate that it is suitable for dessert purposes. We have found in shipping early apples to the West that people pull them before they have reached sufficient growth to continue developing until they have reached a state of maturity. This provision is to meet cases of that kind, and it does it, I think, very fully.

The fruit growers are well organized in different provinces. In the province from which I come, the fruit growers, for a number of years past, have been enforcing regulations as to the grading and marking of fruit. Has this Bill been submitted to the fruit growers, and have any objections been expressed to bringing it into force?

It was submitted to the fruit growers. I believe I stated earlier in the discussion that a conference of fruit growers coming -from all over Canada, from Nova -Scotia to British Columbia, was held in the month of February. They considered this matter for two days, and this Bill is the outcome of their deliberations. I believe that at that conference there were also present a few representatives of the consumers, particularly large companies of
western farmers, handling fruits along with other commodities.

I understood the hon. member for East Lambton to say that one of -the objects of this Bill was to prevent fruit from the United States being distributed in an unfit condition. I see that every package is going to be marked with letters three-quarters of an inch in height before it is taken from the premises in which it is packed. Suppose fruit comes from the other -side of the line and is packed in an immature condition, I do not see this is any protection to the Canadian consumer. I do not see any protection so far for the Canadian consumer.

The fruit to which I refer has been coming in from the United States, and this practice has been followed for years back. Carloads of immature fruit have been brought in year after year from the United States and forced upon the Canadian market and it is a most unwise position for us to be placed in as a people.
How will this Bill prevent that practice5

Because the American exporters of immature fruit will not be allowed to dispose of it in Canada except they conform with the regulations prescribed by this Bill. Not only has the practice to which I have referred been common, but some of our own fruit farmers, in order to get the advantage of the high prices, have been in the habit of shipping immature fruit from their trees and selling it -as wholesome fruit when it is certainly anything but that.
My question had reference to fruit coming across the border in packages. I understood this Bill was designed to protect the Canadian consumer.

There is a law in the United States prohibiting the sale of immature fruit, but when the market over there is denied to the American exporters they ship the immature fruit to this country, just as they do with unmarketable veal and tubercular sheep and hogs.
Does the United States law prevent the exportation of immature fruit?
No.
Then where is there any protection for Canada?

The fruit grown in the United States is subject to inspection there.



When that fruit is rejected, it is shipped to Canada although some of it is unfit for hogs let alone human beings. In the same way they ship to Canada the carcasses of tubercular sheep and hogs that have been rejected over there. They are allowed to do that because the United States will not carry on an inspection for us or for any other outside country-their inspection is intended for the protection of their own people. The clause in the Bill is- aimed at importations into Canada of that class of stuff.
I understand that perfectly, but is there nothing in the present Bill against the shipment of immature, or any other kind of improper fruit, from the United States into Canada?
That is the object of the Bill.

Not the section I have just read 'because it presupposes that the fruit has been shipped in bulk and packed again in Canada. The language of the section is:
Every person who, by himself or through the agency of another person, repacks fruit-
And so on. I do not think there is anything in the Bill to create the presumption that if a man receives a package of immature fruit from the United States that he is creating an agency.

I see your point; how in practice is immature fruit from the United States to 'be held up?
iMt. CRERAR: I may point out to the committee that the purpose of this definition is to prevent the sale of immature fruit.
Fruit that is packed?

It is to insure that fruit that ie immature shall be so stamped and marked so that the purchaser shall know what he is buying. Immature fruit is used very largely for making jams-it has a definite, specific use-but it has happened in the past that immature fruit, for instance, plums and grapes, have been shipped to remote points and -actually sold as good fruit when it was not. The purpose of this definition is merely to make it quite clear that the shipper of fruit,if it is immature, must stamp his basket or package with a label 60 that the purchaser will know what it is he is buying.
Whether it is Canadian or American fruit? fMr. Currie. 1
I think it would apply to American fruit as well, tout -as to that -point I am not absolutely sure.

There are hundreds
of ears of fruit shipped into this country from the United States, which fruit h-as to be picked on the green side or it -would not be in the proper condition to use when it gets here. If the fruit is not picked until it is ri-pe, when it is shipped any distance it cannot be handled at all after reaching its destination. Our company have brought in a great many cars o-f different kinds of fruit f-or the simple reason that we cannot get it here-this country is not producing sufficient fruit. The fruit that we bring into this country, as I say, is picked on the green side, -and 'by the time it reaches its destination in this country it is in a nice condition to handle. If we wait until the fruit has ripened on the tree and then have it shipped, when it reaches here it is in such a condition that we cannot handle it.

I draw the minister's
attention to the fact that the word "Christian" is spelled with a small c throughout the section. That is not as it should be, and I suppose the minister will correct it.

If it has any reference to the -fruit dealers, I would object to the use of the word altogether.
Section -agreed to.
On -section 321 (3)-Package marks:
The -paragraph refers to specimens o-f fruit "of not less than nearly medium size and some colour for the variety," etc. Should that not he "same colour."

"Some" is right.
On paragraph 321-subsection 7-Fruit unfit for use:	-

This section provides that no persons shall sell or expose for sale any fruit in any "package" that is diseased, wormy or otherwise depreciated. Would it not be just as bad if the dealer had this diseased fruit in bulk, and not in a package? It would seem that he could have it in as bad a condition as he likes if it is not in a package, but that it is only when it is in a package that the law applies.

It seems to me that this section will affect the, sale of fruit which is quite general at certain times of the year in certain sections of Eastern Canada. For instance, take the blueberry season: Young folks go out and gather blueberries, bring

them in in pails, and sell them. The same thing is done in the raspberry season. Apparently "no person shall sell, or offer, expose or have in his possession for sale any fruit in any package"-even in an open package-intended for sale unless marked as required by this section. I do not think the minister intends that the village children who pick strawberries, raspberries or blueberries have to mark the package to dispose of them among their friends in the village.
If the hon. member will look at paragraph (b) of section 319, he will note that it is provided that " 'fruit' shall not include wild fruit, nor cranberries, whether wild or cultivated."
That provision will protect the sale I have mentioned.
This Bill does not refer to that.

Paragraph agreed to.
On paragraph 325-Fruit packages:

I observe that this Bill provides that all these fruits shall be sold in packages of a certain size, a made-to-order package, of specified length, width and depth, taper, etc. To my mind it is difficult to comply with that law. Why should these fruits not also be sold by the pail or by the bag, unless for wholesale or export purposes, when there would be some object in making a fixed size of package in which a commodity should be sold? For instance, in the following section I notice that currants shall be sold in containers of four-fifths of a quart, and that a pint box. shall be four and three-eighths by four and three-eighths at top and bottom and one and seven-eighths inches deep, and m on. It will take a Philadelphia lawyer to interpret what all this means. -We have been in the habit of selling these fruits in pails, baskets, bags, or barrels. I do not see the gain in this legislation, or the possibility of dealing with it. It is absolutely impossible for a small dealer throughout the country to sell his fruits in accordance with this Bill.
I do not agree with the bon. gentleman. What we want is standard size baskets.
You are a wholesale dealer, and I am not.
I am a large buyer.

I am not selling to large buyers, and you are selling to me.
142J

Your neighbour wants to know what he is getting. If he is buying a standard basket, then he will know. I quite agree that this clause is a move in the right direction. I am a canner, and we are trying to standardize our cans all the way through, jam can, fruit can and vegetable can; we are doing that now, and I can see' a great advantage by doing so. I do not see why the same thing should not apply to these fruits.	.

Let me give the hon. gentleman a concrete instance. Take a farmer; living outside of Aylmer, who does not want to sell to large wholesale organizations, but to the retail merchant. By this Bill he is supposed to sell fruits in packages of specified dimensions. How will he get the baskets? Why should he not sell the fruit as he does now, in pails, or sell his apples by the bag, as he has been doing?

I can tell you why. I think it is the small buyer we are looking after. The large buyeT can take care of himself better than the small buyer. This is a protection to the boy, or the girl, or the housewife who buys one package of . fruit. I cannot get away from that. I think it is a splendid move, and one in the right direction.	.

It is a move that these multi-millionaires invariably have against the poor, downtrodden boy and girl in the country:	It is almost impossible
for every farmer to have a package or measure of this kind at his disposal at all times. Time and again we have provided 'that bags of certain capacity shall be used and that certain products shall be sold in certain kinds of measures. This limiting the size and shape of every measure that articles are sold in is all piffle. For the wholesale trade, let the requirements be up to a certain standard; let the measure be described as a bushel, peck, quart, or pint. But under this provision, a farmer is violating the law if he sells fruit in a bushel which is an inch too long and a corresponding inch too narrow.

This clause is in the interests of consumers. We have standard size barrels in Ontario. The people of Nova Scotia have the same, and they are unable to sell apples in the United States because their barrel is of such a size that it does not conform with the regulations in the United States. The small boxes in which cherries and berries and smaller fruits are packed are supplied by

large manufacturers. It is very easy for the farmers to conform to certain regulations respecting the size of the packages. Fruit men throughout the country are anxious that these standard boxes should be in universal use.
Mr, FEASEE: I take exception to this clause respecting the baskets. In the Niagara Falls district we have had for the past two years a basket manufactured of paper; it has ho tacks in it. A large order has been received for the supplying of baskets of this, kind to the British trade. It is one of the best baskets on the market. As long as the basket is of a standard size and of strong construction, I do not see that it makes any difference what shape it is.

Is the hon.
gentleman referring to packages of fruit for export?
No, to packages to be sold in our own markets.
What is the objection to conforming with these regulations?
Because this basket has no tacks in it; you cannot put tacks in the bottom of it.

Take the case of a village of 300 or 500 inhabitants around which there is a farming community. The farmers have small quantities of strawberries and apples to sell and it is a great convenience to them to be able to bring this fruit to town and sell it by the pint, quart or gallon. There is also an advantage to the purchaser, because he knows what he is getting; besides, he gets the fruit in convenient form. For shipping purposes it is all right to provide such a standard as is specified in the Bill, but some provision should be made to meet- cases of the kind to which I refer.
'Mr. CUEEIE:	Does not most of the
trouble arise because in Canada we use an Imperial measure, while in the United States they use what is known as the wine measure? In the United States the strawberry box contains, say, a wine quart- we call it wine measure in this country-while in Canada we have the Imperial quart, which is one fifth larger. That places the Canadian dealer at a disadvantage, because in the United States they will not give him credit for the additional amount contained in his package. Are the measures spoken of in this provision with refer-

ence to pears, crab apples, plum.s, and so on, based on the number of cubic inches contained in a quart or in a peck as the case may be; or are they simply arbitrary measurements?

I think that the following provision of section 327 covers the objection of the member for Welland (Mr. Fraser):
Every basket of fruit packed in Canada, for sale in Canada, and every basket manufactured and offered for sale in Canada, of other material than wood veneer shall be of such dimensions as may be specified by the Minister of Agriculture, and shall contain, when level full, as nearly as practicable, one or other of the following quantities.

That is all right for the large dealers, but we are legislating not for the large dealers, but for the ordinary farmers. Half the fruit sold in Canada is disposed of by small farmers, who peddle it around in the villages and small towns. Under this provision, if a farmer sells a pail of cherries, that does not comply with the law, he is a criminal. That should not be, because the transaction is absolutely straight and square and fair. It is all right to provide that -fruit for export shall be put in a package of a certain size, but when a man is selling in small quantities direct to the consumer, let him sell it in the most convenient way and for whatever he can get.
Mr. (BALL: Fruit for export or for shipment to a point some considerable distance away ought to be put in packages, boxps or barrels, but when it is locally disposed of it is quite unnecessary to adopt the method suggested by this provision. Moreover, the added expense is unnecessary. The measurement. Imperial gallon, or any other measurement, is not, as I understand it, a consideration. The size of the boxes is defined. But for local consumption, it is unnecessary to go to the expense of putting up fruit in boxes or barrels, unless people wish to have it put up in that manner.

If the hon. member will refer to section 326, he will see that it mentions the word " bushels." Subsection 2 says:
Every wood veneer basket of fruit packed in fana.i'i f.j s-n'e in Canada, or manufactured

and offered for sale in Canada, shall contain, when level full, as- nearly as practicable, one or other of the following quantises :-
(a)	one bushel;
(b)	eleven quarts.
And so on.

The ordinary farmer who has, say, ten quarts of fruit knows that in the fruiit season farmers and their wives come into the market with a pail of cherries, a pail of plums, a pail of apples, and so on. That is the half-basket. Why should such people be penalized because that is the custom they have always followed? They have only a small quantity of fruit. They are not wholesale dealers or multi-millionaires. I do not know that anybody will enforce this law with regard to them, but why should they be made liable to a penalty, made criminals according to the law, for selling in small quantities, as their ancestors have done for generations? If their pail does not conform with the exact measurements of the bushel measure as set forth in this legislation, such people would be liable.

They are
allowed to sell in that way.
Not as II read the section.

I realize that there is some force in the point raised by the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes). Possibly an exception might be considered in the case of a farmer or fruit grower who brings fruit into the market and sells direct to the consumer.
Hear, hear.

That point, as I interpret this section, is not covered. On the other hand, if a fruit grower, no matter whether he be doing business in a large or a small way, is selling to a retailer who resells to the consumer, he should be obliged to sell in baskets or packages.
Or the retailer should be obliged to put the fruit into baskets or packages.
I think we should have to start a little further back than the retailer. I would suggest that this section stand, and I shall look into that point and bring it up again later on.

I am very much obliged. The man whom I have in mind is not the fruit grower as such. I do not know what the definition of the term " fruit grower " is. But I mean the man who has
a farm, behind which he hias an orchard with some plum, apple and cherry trees, and who makes a few hundred dollars a year out of his fruit. There are thousands of such farmers throughout Ontario and the Maritime Provinces. Those farmers could not possibly comply with this legislation, and I want them to be protected from being made criminals under it.
At one o'clock the House rose.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

I'.beg to move to amend section 326 by striking out the words "issue permits" and substituting therefor the words "make regulations." This- will cover the point raised by my hon. friend from Victoria.
Would it not be better to leave -the section just as it is and add the words "make regulations-?" That would enable the -minister to cover -any cas-es that came up.

I think my amendment
is better.

I do not want to
hold up the Bill at all, but there is danger in rushing through legislation in the last days of the session. This Bill, for instance, in my opinion will cause any amount of trouble to local sellers, and they will not put up with being inconvenienced in this way. What is the. bushel mentioned here? Is it the same as the grain bushel?
Imperial measure.
Is our standard grain bushel the Imperial measure?

It must be the
same-.

I mention that just to illustrate the difficulties the minister will be up against all over the country. If the two bushels, -are not the same, people will be- -selling wheat by one- bushel and fruit by another, -and it will cause any amount of confusion. I would suggest that the local men might dispose of their fruit to the retailer without having to- comply with these provisions-. What is to prevent my hon. friend from Elgin, for instance, buying -all the stuff that comes along in pails, half-pails or quarter-pails, and having his men put it into packages? Let that be the business of the man who sells- to the general public. I fully endorse the idea of having packages, -but it will le-ad to all sorts of trouble to men who sell locally.

I would point out that wild fruit is excluded from the application of these previsions 'by the definition of the word fruit, and I think the amendment I have moved will cover the point raised by my hon. friend. I do not know whether he intends1 that those people in the Niagara district, for instance, who are growing fruit as a business and selling it as part of their regular farm product should ibe permitted to sell their fruit in packages to suit themselves.
No, I do not.

Then we have to meet the requirement of the farmer who raises a little fruit and may take it into the local town to sell it direct to the consumer. There is a provision in the latter part of this section:	-
That the said Minister may issue permits allowing any person or persons to use packages of other sizes than those specified in the foregoing section.
1 have proposed an amendment to that, so that we may frame regulations to cover these particular cases.
All right.

One remark made by the hon. member for Victoria strikes me as singularly appropriate, and that is that legislation like this, which is extremely desirable and brings this whole matter out of chaos into order, should be considered very carefully. For my part I venture to say this House should do as it .did last year, adjourn to meet again in the summer. The men are sweating in the trenches; loi us do some sweating here. Why should we try to get rid of our duties at the earliest possible moment and clear out of here as soon as we possibly can? For my part, I am not a farmer, and may not be doing very much here, but I would say, let us stay right here and do our duty fully.
Go and work on your farm.

Section agreed to.
On section 331-penalty for destroying or pilfering fruit:

This section says:
Every person who carelessly handles, wilfully destroys or pilfers any fruit packed in any of the packages prescribed in this Part shall be guilty of an offence and1 liable upon summary conviction to a penalty not exceeding twenty-five dollars.
It seems to me to be wrong to put careless handling on the same basis as thieving, for pilfering is thieving.
It says, "not exceeding twenty-five dollars." A magistrate could fine lightly or up to the limit.

Section agreed to.
On section 337A-potato grades:
Is there anything in this section to prevent a man selling potatoes and letting the buyer grade them?
No.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

House again in Committee on Bill No. 19, to amend the Inspection and Sale Act (vegetables, eggs, food containers, firewood and cement)-Sir	George	Foster.-Mr. Boivm in the Chair.

That clause 360b be struck out.

Motion agreed to.
On section 4-Act not to apply to articles now in stock; date of coming into force:
That is not necessary now, as it is included in the new clause 358 (d). I therefore beg to move that it be struck out.

On section 5-Date of coming into force:

I move that there shall be substituted for that section the following:

On section 2 (358 a)-Packages of food and containers to be marked:
On motion of St. George Foster, the Committee reverted to section 358a.

It will be remembered that when we were discussing packing or labelling of milk in bottles it seemed as though we ought to amend that clause
otherwise it would be necessary for some permanent stamp to be aflixed to or blown into the bottle. I propose to make that clear in the same manner as has been done

In Acts of this kind in the United States. I therefore move:
That at the end of the 25th line; after the word "branded'' there be added the words "or otherwise indicated on the outside or top or on a label or tag: attached thereto."
This will make it easy to affix the label to the bottle or to attach an independent label thereto. ,

According to the amendment made by the minister to section 5, this Act will not come into force until one year after it has received the Royal Assent. But before that another clause was amended to provide that stock on hand would not be affected by the provisions of the Act. What is the use of amending the two clauses in this way if the Act is to come into force within one year after it has received the Royal Assent? His amendment would be useless, as far as I can see if it does not cover all the stock.

The amendment of which I gave notice to section 358 D provides that:
This Act does not apply to any articles held in stock by wholesale or retail dealers prior to the coming into force of the Act.
If, when the Act comes into force, he shall have a stock on hand, this Act shall not apply to it. That gives a wide privilege and at the same time it takes away any reason for discontent as to his having to remark articles which he .may have in stock. Then the amendment proceeds to state other exceptions from the operation of the Act:
The .provisions of this Act shall not apply.-
(e)	To packages containing two avoirdupois ounces, or less, which packages shall be exempt from marking in terms of weight;
(f)	To packages containing one fluid ounce, or less, which packages shall be exempt from marking in terms of measure.
These are very small articles, and it is not considered worth while to bother with them, or to insist on their (being, labelled with measurements, weights, or names.
(g)	to any article the sale of which as regards the weight or marking thereof is already provided for under other statutes.
We do not want to duplicate the legislation.
(h)	those food oommoditles which may at the time this Act comes into force, or which thereafter may be subject to any regulation or order of the Canada Food Control Board as respects the weight of such commodity or the weight or proportion of ingredients used in the manufacture of such commodity.
We do not wish to interfere with the work of the Pood Board in making these changes
and regulations from time to time. These are extraordinary regulations adopted by the Food Board and they are called for by the necessities and circumstances of war conditions. We do not bind them down by the letter of this enactment. But while the war continues and while the work of the Food Board is going on, this clause is necessary.
(i)	those food commodities held' in stock at the time that such regulations of the Canada Food Board referred to in paragraph (h) become inoperative.
That avoids the confusion and expense of relabelling, remarking, reweighing, and remeasuring the stock that may be on hand at that particular time. .
This part of the Act applying to imported goods will interfere with the importation of food.
No, it does not interfere with the importation of food.
It does interfere with it if we set up a standard in this country which is not the standard in the United States.
We must have our own standard.

The packers in the
United States will pack in accordance with their standard and not in accordance with our standard, and there will he trouble in connection with the importation of goods packed in that way.
The importer will' have the advantage of a whole year to order his imports and to see that they are packed according to these regulations. It is not necessary to wait for a year to put in the order.

This will have the effect of increasing prices if we do not have the same standard as they have in the United States. The packers in the United States will have to pack goods specially for our trade, they .will have to charge for that, *and it will mean higher prices to our consumers. All food products aTe high enough now. We are anxious to keep down prices and to reduce the cost of living, hut by this legislation we are putting prices up.

I do not think that myself. The object of the legislation is- to make it sure that the consumer when he buys shall know what he is getting and what he is paying for. It would be unfair, as my bon. friend will see, to have a lesser measure put up in bottles or packages

in another country, say the United States, and have those bottles and packages come here and compete, on the same outward appearances, with a larger measure which our own packers and our makers put up. We simply guard ourselves in the interest of the Canadian consumer, that is all.

THE TAKING OF THE SOKDEEKjS' VOTE AT LAST ELECTION.
On the motion, of Hon. A. K. Maclean that the House go into Committee -of Supply.

On Saturday last, I notified the Prime Min-isted that I intended to discuss on the first convenient opportunity a matter I considered of .some importance, and as I have not heard from him, I presume it is satisfactory to him to proceed this afternoon. The matter, IMr. Speaker, I desire to bring to the attention of Parliament is in reference to the taking of the soldiers' votes in th-e elections held on December 17 last.

Ilf my hon. friend will excuse me, it is stated that there was an understanding that this matter should not come up until to-morrow. The Prime Minister, especially, wished to he present.
I am not sure whether my hon. friend expected, or understood, that he should receive- word with reference to it. He -says he has not, and, of course, that goes without saying. But if he has not, it was from a misunderstanding or -some little neglect. The Prime Minister is engaged this afternoon on a very important matter with high authorities in -connection with our defence. Under the circumstances, if my hon. friend would -allow it to go over until to-morrow h-e would consult very much the convenience of the Prime Minister.

The Prime Minister asked me to confer with him regarding the business of the House, and going over the various -matters I informed him that we intended to bring up the

matter of the soldiers' votes, about which my hon. friend from Westmorland had notified him. The Prime Minister told me that perhaps it would be more convenient for him to have the discussion to-morrow.
1 understand that the Prime Minister did not intend to take part in the discussion.
I immediately notified my hon. friend (Mr. Copp) that he might he called upon to postpone his motion until to-morrow. Under the circumstances, we cannot refuse to accede to the request that the discussion of this matter Ibe postponed, but in view of the fact that the time of the House may be well taken up to-morrow with the debate on titles, and possibly other matters. I suggest that if this motion be not proceeded with tomorrow afternoqn, it be taken up on Wednesday morning.	*
I am muchobliged to my right hon. friend.
As I have said, I communicated with the Prime Minister regarding my intention to make this motion, and as I did not hear from him, I supposed that it was all right to go on with it.
It is understood, then, that if it is too- late to take this matter up to-morrow afternoon, we shall proceed with it the first thing Wednesday morning?
Yes.'
Motion agreed to, and the House went into Committee of Supply.

Trade and Commerce-Trade commissioners and commercial agents, including expenses in connection with negotiations of treaties or in extension of commercial relations'; miscellaneous advertising and printing, or other expenditure connected with the extension of Canadian trade, $160,000. .
['Supply.']
Has anything been done to implement the report made by the commission sent to France?

Since the commission made their report, congestion in France as well as on the seas has increased rather than diminished. The facilities which in normal times are used/ for the exchange of commercial products1 have been devoted to the transport of food', munitions and other war necessities. Trade has been entirely stopped in a great many lines and greatly interrupted in all. The commission made a thorough investigation and published their information in a very instructive way. Under the circumstances, it has not been possible to do more than that.
The report is a splendid one.

It has been distributed broadcast amongst onr traders, businessman and producers. It is impossible to push trade with warring countries at this time, if we except trade in such commodities and articles as are necessary for the war. As these things are largely bought by the governments themselves, private business transactions between the inhabitants of all countries have been disarranged.
I suppose the same applies to our Russian business.
Worse.

A very interesting report was published by the department some time ago with regard to the possibilities of Canadian trade with Russia and Siberia. Tne other day I inquired whether the Government were aware of the denunciation by France of the Franco-Canadian Treaty. I have seen in the press that France lias denounced all her trade treaties. In the British House of Commons the other day Mr. Bonar Law or Mr. Balfour said that as a result of the. Paris Economic Conference, France had denounced all her treaties. The Prime Minister said, in reply to my inquiry, that he was not aware of any such denunciation. I wish now to renew my -question. Our trade with France during the existence of the Franco-Canadian treaty was particularly extensive in connection with the importation to Canada of French wines.
Now that we have established prohibition in Canada, the French trade will thereby suffer to a large extent, although we can do business with the French people in other ways. It seems to me that, after the visit of that commission on the other side and by .the report of that commission, we can, after the war, establish much closer trade relations with Prance. We should have, as they have in the United Kingdom, commercial agents not only in Paris, but in other laTge French cities, such as Bordeaux, Nantes, Marseilles, Lyons, and possibly Rouen. The war will have brought France and England so close to one .another that this country should, by reason of its national traditions, help in maintaining the entente cordiale between France and England, and although sentiment and business are two different things, yet I believe a good commercial treaty and sound business relations will help to maintain the happy friendship that exists between the Mother Country -and France.

I do not know if my right hon. friend has the latest figures as regards the trade between France and Canada, but the present large trade is, of course, due to wax conditions. At the same time, one must admit that France has, during the present war, been an extraordinarily good customer of Canada. Our trade statistics will show that very plainly. Before the war the total trade, exports and imports, between the two countries was relatively small, but since 1914 we have become one of the great allies of France from the commercial standpoint alone, not to speak of other standpoints. We are now selling to France in the millions, whilst we ourselves continue to buy from France at a much lower figure. I do not expect that, in the years to come, our imports from France will equal our exports, neither do the French people expect that. But from my conversation with some of the French consuls in this country, I am led to believe .that if the Government, in particular the Minister of Trade and Commerce, will help in this connection we may establish a buoyant, permanent trade with France.

When the question with reference to the denunciation of treaties was put to the House by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) a week or so ago, no official information had reached the Government of the action that had been taken. Since that 4 p.m. time official information has reached the Government, and Frrnce has given notice of the termination of all her treaties with all countries. With reference to Canada, as I suppose is the case with reference to other countries, the notice runs "from the 15th of May." One year after the 15th of May, the treaties will be denounced. But the statement is also made that in the denunciation of the treaties, it is not the intention of France to terminate favoured arrangements with those nations with whom she has had relations before, but that the denunciation of the treaties takes place in order to put France, under the altered conditions, in the position of making new arrangements with the different countries. France is not alone in respect to that action. Great Britain is following the same course, and so I imagine are most of the other nations.
What about Japan?

I would, however, prefer not to give the reason for the denunciation of the treaties to be the basis which was laid down in the resolutions 	-
adopted by the Economic Conference at Paris; rather the resolutions adopted in that conference and the denunciation of those treaties arise from the very same circumstances-the necessity for our grading and rearranging commercial relations owing to the world-wide dislocation of trade brought about by the war.
We had commenced an excellent propaganda in Russia. We had one of our most expert trade commissioners at Petrograd, and a very bright and capable young man at Omsk. Both of those gentlemen had about a year or a year and a half of work in their respective localities, but the collapse of the Russian government in so far as carrying on the war was concerned, and the widespread confusion which took place thereafter, the utter congestion of trade transport inland and the almost utter lack of ocean transport, have made it necessary that both those gentlemen should be recalled from their positions. Mr. Just has lately arrived, fortunately safely, in England, and Mr. Wilgress is now at work for the department in the southern part of China, with his headquarters at Hong Kong. He will probably remain there until matters settle down in Russia sufficiently to-enable him to take up his work again from anything like an advantageous position. All our trade commissioners have been interfered with in their work largely by the confusion of transport and of trade conditions.
At the same time they have been diligently at work gathering information and preparing reports, which are being distributed, and endeavouring in every possible way to prepare for the coming better period by keeping the relations between business men here and business men in those other countries as far as possible intact.

What about my
suggestion that after the war more commercial agents be appointed in those large centres? I do. not mean that my hon. friend is not doing the needful as far as Paris is concerned, although everybody who has travelled in Europe knows that the commissioners in Paris and1 London are not able to look after the trade of Canada, because Canadians abroad simply overwhelm their offices with requests for information of all kinds. It seems to me we should have- we had them in Germany before the war- agents on the continent and especially in France, at such places as Rouen, Lyons, Marseilles, Bordeaux, whose special business would be to develop the trade between

Canada and France. One agent in Paris is not sufficient for the whole of France.

I quite agree,
hut the only thing that can be done at the moment is for the department to keep a watchful eye on what happens. One thing is quite certain, and that is that methods and' opportunities for interchange will be very largely altered by reason of the war, and agencies in France may be taken advantage of which have not been available heretofore; such, for instance, as the Lyons' fair, which takes place every year and which will open up an excellent opportunity, when times become more normal,' for representation of our wares to the representative business men of France, leading up to business connections. It is true that France is buying largely -from us -at the present time and selling comparatively little to us, but the balance of trade, while in our favour at the present time, is largely a fictitious one and does not represent anything permanent. In peace times the balance of trade was very largely in favour of France who sent us many millions of dollars' worth of goods more than we sent to her, so the balance is now righting itself. What will happen after the war will depend very largely upon the basic needs of France in relation to our sources of. large supply. For instance, France o-ught to take from Canada a great amount of lumber and other material for reconstruction purposes. That is all being noted as carefully as possible by the department, and when the proper time com-es these matters will all be taken up. In the meantime nothing -can be done in the way of negotiations.

I would ask the minister, if he attends the Imperial Conference, or if he does not, his colleagues, to look especially after the interests of Canadian trade. It is true that a Canadian business man abroad can always rely on the British consulates to protect him and give all the information he requires in his trade. But England is a nation of shopkeepers, be it said without derogation, and looks after her own business through her consulates. The question has been brought up on several occasions in the House. Perhaps it would be possible for this Government to have in those British consulates on the continent, and especially in* France, Canadian attaches who would" especially represent the interests- of Canadian trade. Let my hon. friend understand me well; I do not wish to break the tie between the Mother Country
and Canada, but this is a cold-blooded business proposition, and it seems to me that with all our natural and industrial resources we should do more ini the after.-the-war period to advertise our wares and our business than we have done heretofore.
If we had Canadian attaches in the British consulates on the continent, I think our trade would certainly be the gainer. My hon. friend is quite correct in saying that in view of the world revolution going on our trade at the present time is largely fictitious, tout even during this- revolutionary period, by taking the tide which leads on to fortune, Canada can build up a trade in connection with reconstructing the devastated areas in France, for instance, which I think would be of lasting advantage to this country. Look at what the Americans have done. Two years ago a conference of American business men and capitalists was called in the city of Boston, and all American business and industrial concerns were invited to unite in an effort to capture all the trade that would develop in reconstructing the devastated areas of France. I do not know whether my hon. friend followed that matter very closely, but a copy of the programme issued by the association came into my hands last year.
I cannot see why the Americans should get -preference over the Canadians in this line of business. I do not know why our business men from Toronto, Montreal, and other large industrial centres should not reap the benefits American business men are enjoying. They are rebuilding the cities and towns and villages in France which have been recaptured from the Germans by the Allied armies. Only the other day I read a very interesting article to the effect that the Quakers, whose tenets will not allow them to take part with the combatant armies, are going to help the Red Cross and help reconstruct the devastated villages and towns.
(Sir THOMAS WHITE, Minister of Finance, having entered the House after a prolonged absence through illness, and being warmly, greeted toy hon. members),

I hope I express the feeling of the House in welcoming back our hon. friend the Minister of Finance. Mr. Chairman, I would ask my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce to take note of the few remarks I -have made. They -are made in earnest. It seems to me that with pluck and with true sturdy Cana-dianism we should a-t least equal the Americans in capturing war trade. I call it war trade because it is trade that has developed

as a consequence of the war, but it will be lasting, (because the reconstruction period will extend over a number of years. the extension of trade and banking facilities must go hand in hand. Probably we have suffered in thalt respect as a young country. What is this Dominions Royal Commission?
In 1912 there was issued by the British Government a Royal Commission, consisting of representatives from the self-governing Dominions and the United Kingdom.

The hon. member mentions one of the volumes. There is another volume, which, I think, is. equally important. There is not extant to-day a statistical statement with the same modernity, the 6a,me grasp and scope, as. the statistics compiled and issued in that volume. Not only does it contain the best of the published statistics of each country, but it has those supplemented by actual investigations made by the commissioners themselves in all those countries, and special statistical tables with reference to different lines of production, resources and such things, which information does, not exist in any other statistics.
And about the ports?

Yes, about all those things. Besides that, there are in the addenda, most valuable and exhaustive reports upon most of the great lines of activity, given by eminent engineers and ether eminent authorities, which reports lie there as a veritable thesaurus, a treasure-house of fact, which you could not get anywhere else. I make that statement here so that hon. members, who take an interest in those things, may have their attention directed to the report. That commission arose, as the committee knows, out of the deliberations and conclusions of an Imperial Conference.

Whatever was the purpose of the conference, whether it was to avoid a difficulty or whether it was to have a difficulty solved by a better medium than the simple cogitations of the members of the commission sitting in London for a few days or a few weeks, that commission started on a recommendation of the Imperial Conference of 1911. That report goes back to the British Government, and it will be submitted to the Imperial Conference when it next meets. Some of the suggestions of the Dominions Royal Commission have already been embodied, in whole or in part, in action which has already been taken by the British Government.

But here again you come to a time of flux. For the reconstruction period, you have, in those statistics and in that information, the best and the only large fundamental basis of information which will be so valuable for reconstruction purposes. value so far as permanent and normal conditions are concerned.

All of our agents, I understand, in the United States carry out very much the siame work. We have agents located at -something like eighteen points in the United States. In addition to that, there are at all of our agencies a great many inquiries made with respect to many matters relating to Canada, and our officials are there for the purpose of furnishing persons seeking information with any information which it is possible for them to give. These offices are only established for the purpose of disseminating information regarding Canada.

It occurred to me that possibly at this time, when there is very little immigration, some of these offices might be discontinued. I am free to admit that it is quite possible that they may be doing effective work. But I would like to draw to the attention of the minister one instance at least, of an immigration officer who is, I think, rather exceeding his duties, that is the case of the officer at Philadelphia about whom I had a question on the order paper this morning, a man

who took a most active -and offensive part in the conduct of the elections, writing partisan articles in a paper of which he was formerly the editor. -It seems to me that it would be the duty of the department to curb actions of that kind on the part of any official of the Government. I refer to Mr. Jaffray of Philadelphia.

I may say, Mr. Chairman, that I thoroughly agree with what the hon. member has said. It is only recently that that matter was brought to my attention. I think it is very unfortunate that any officer in the position which Mr. Jaffray occupies should undertake to write articles to the press of the nature complained of in this House, and I certainly disapprove of any such conduct on the part of any official of the department. I have the matter under consideration and am endeavouring to get the exact facts.
With reference to the- general statement that there is no work being done in the United Stat-ee at the present time in the way of securing immigrants for -Canada, I can assure the hon. gentleman that that is not correct. As a matter of fact, some-ting like 75,000 people came to Canada from the United States last year, and that is a very large number. And there is a possibility from the outlook at the present time that we will have even a larger immigration from the United States this year. As a matter of fact, our agencies are quite busy and doing good work there. Our work in the Old Country and in Europe has, of course, practically ceased. I might also say that, as- regards our work in the United States, it is my intention during the year to have all of our agencies thoroughly inspected with a view to seeing what economies can be effected. I feel we can effect a good many economies in that direction, just as we will be able to do in Canada itself. We have a very large staff. A good many duties have been added to the immigration -staff in Canada during the course of the last two years. Nevertheless I feel that if the matter is carefully inquired into we can utilize the staff as a whole on a much more efficient basis, and effect a good many economies. In eo far as our agencies in the United States are concerned they will all be very carefully reviewed during the present season.
Mr. McMAlSTER:	May I ask the minister whether any statistics are kept in his department which would enable him to advise the committee as to the number of immigrants which originate in the territory served by the different offices, and the

cost of operating the offices from which the immigrants in question originate? If such statistics could be kept it would be of great assistance to the House in deciding whether these very considerable sums of money are really justified. Take the case of this Philadelphian agent, who writes offensive partisan .articles for a paper in western Ontario; it would be interesting to know what his salary was and how many Philadelphians through his eloquence and persuasive powers were induced to come to Canada. And that principle, if followed in all the offices, would enable the minister to advise the House, and enable the House to judge, as to whether the country was really getting value for this money.

I hardly think that these offices as at present constituted wouid be able to furnish that information. However,
I shall take my hon. friend's suggestion into consideration.
Mr. MoMASTER: We should have some check on these immigrants with a view to finding out where they come from. For instance, if we spent $10,000 on an agency in Pennsylvania and for three or four years no immigrants come to Canada from that state, the offioe in that state would not be worth the amount expended.

The suggestion that offices of that kind might be dispensed with arose from the fact that the gentleman spoken of, an official of. the department, apparently does not devote all his time to promoting immigration and colonization for Canada.
I am glad to know that the minister intends to look into, this matter.
When was Mr. Jaffray appointed in Philadelphia?

Within the last two or three years, I think.
Contingencies in Canadian, British and foreign agencies, and general immigration expenses! $550,000.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: How much of that is spent in Europe?
I have not that information before me, hut if the hon. gentleman is .anxious to have it I will bring it down.
In a general way, what /are' these contingencies ?

The large items include: advertising, $240,000; printing, $45,000; expenses of our agencies in the United States, $100,000; expenses of our agencies in Great Britain, $50,000; location of settlers, $25,-
000; boundary expenses, $35,000; deportation expenses, $10,000, a total of $505,000. The balance is made up by a great variety of small items.
Is this advertising in Canadian newspapers?
In the papers of United States, Great Britain and, to some extent, Canada.
We are getting no immigrants from Europe; why should we spend so much money on advertising in Great Britain?

Only a small amount of
advertising is done there at present. Two or three years ago the expenditure on immigration work was about $1,900,000. A reduction of $800,000 was effected and this year we are cutting the expenditure down by a further $100,000. If we wish to undertake immigration work in Great Britain after the war it is necessary that we maintain our organization there, and that a limited amount of advertising be done in order to keep Canada's possibilities before the people of that .country. During the present year I hope to be able to go to England with a view to finding out what the actual conditions are. I am advised New Zealand, Australia, and the other dominions are carrying on a very active propaganda, and we may have to spend imore money if we wish to secure the results after the war that every person in the country is looking for.
What staffs have you in Great Britain and in foreign countries?

We have twelve offices in the British Islands. The total staff numbers about sixty, thirty-five of whom are in London. Most of these offices were opened many years ago. The'staffs of all the offices have been cut down to a minimum. Our offices in United Kingdom-this applies particularly to the office in London-have been exceedingly busy during the last two years.
One can understand that, with the large number of Canadians overseas, theTe are a great many who frequent those offices The officers have charge of all the booking arrangements for those, apart from so'diers, who are coming to Canada, and at times they have been exceedingly busy and have had to add to their staffs in order to cope with the work which they are undertaking. As an illustration, I might mention a case that occurred not long ago. The British Admiralty sent word to the commissioner that they had a boat available for two or

Might I ask the minister if, in addition to endeavouring to secure immigration from the British Isles, the United States and some other countries, he will endeavour to bring Belgians to Canada? Only yesterday I received, from a gentleman at present in France, a letter stating that many of the Belgian refugees in France contemplated taking up land in Canada if 'land were available. I need not tell my hon. friend that the Belgian is a very desirable settler, not only for the prairies hut as a market gardener. Wherever you find a Belgian around a city, you will find a splendid garden and a hardworking man, intelligently cultivating the land and supplying the market with garden produce. We have an opportunity of inducing many of those refugees, both in France and in England, to come to Canada, and I would advise the minister to look after that Belgian immigration. We know that Belgium is small in area and can hardly maintain the large population which it had before the war, and with all the patriotism that honours the Belgians, it is to be expected that thousands of them will prefer to come to the United States or to Canada to returning to their own country. I would advise my hon. friend to appoint a special agent to interview those people in England and France in order to capture our share of that most desirable class of immigration.

The matter to. which my hon. friend alludes will receive attention.
