Administration of Chinese Immigration- salaries, $24,(WO, contingencies, $5,000.
I should like to know where the men are located for whom we are voting $24,000, and what their duties are.

The officials are located at Victoria, Vancouver, Union Bay, Powell River, and Chemainus, in British Columbia, and at Montreal in the province of Quebec. The total number of officials employed is twenty, and their duties are in connection with Chinese immigrants entering or attempting to enter Canada. It is their duty to see that the regulations and restrictions on Chinese immigration are complied with. There are seven officials in Victoria and eleven in Vancouver, including clerks and stenographers.	.

After what happened last year does the minister expect there will be a greater Chinese immigration this year than last? Is a patrol maintained on the border to prevent the smuggling into Canada of Chinese, and what officials are guarding against this smuggling? I understand there is an organization of detectives or other employees engaged in this work.

We have about 200 or. 250 inspectors along the boundary, and it is their duty to prevent any person, whether Chinese or not, entering Canada who is not entitled to come in under the law. Speaking offhand, I think last year there were about 16,000 rejections of intending immigrants to Canada, who were not permitted to come in under the law. I would imagine that all our boundary inspectors have been instructed to see that no Chinese come in who are not entitled to do: so. .
I was told by an official of the department that after a certain date Chinamen were not allowed to enter this country. Are they still coming in?
Yes. Some five hundred or so came in last year.

Referring to the item of general immigration expenses, is it still the policy of the department to distribute among the schools of foreign countries, more particularly of Great Britain, the atlas that has been sent out a number of years showing the size and resources of the different provinces of Canada? I am fold it was a very useful method, of advertising our country.

The policy is still being carried out in Great Britain, and to a lesser extent in the United States. After the war broke out we cut down our expenses in Great Britain, and as a result the distribution has not been as large as in former years. I intend during the present year to review carefully the whole question of the preparation and distribution of literature not only in Great Britain but in the United

States as well. We have spent large sums of money in that direction, and I think every effort should be made to get as much value as we can from this class of expenditure.
Supplementary estimates 1917-18-Department of Immigration and Colonization-to provide for the salary of the Private Secretary from October 12, 1917, at the rate of $2,500 per annum, $1,176.06.
His salary is included in the main estimates. He is in subdivision B of the first division.
Item No. 326 in the Supplementary Estimates is to provide for the private secretary at $2,500?
Yes.
The secretary for whom we are voting this salary now has no other official position! in the department? This is to provide for the secretary of the minister?'

Yes.
Civil Government-Privy Council Office-* salaries, $44,900, contingencies, $10,000.

I see.
1st division, sub-division A: -Assistant clerk of Privy Council at $4,000.
Who is the Assistant Clerk of the Privy Council and when was he appointed?

Mr. Bennetts, who has
been in the Privy Council office for over thirty years, and is one of the oldest officials in the office.
When was he appointed?
I do not know, but he was appointed long before I became President of the Privy Council.
There is the assistant clerk at $4,000, and another at $3,925. To whom does the latter item refer?
That refers to one of the clerks in the department, Mr. Mackenzie, who has been there for a great many years.

Then I see:
2nd division, sub-division A: one at $2,100; one at $1,850; one at $1,625.
I would like to know who these clerks are. Are they old clerks who are being increased, or are they new appointments? Take, for instance, four at $2,600 in the First Division subdivision B.
These four are old clerks in the department, and it is proposed to advance one, Mr. Belanger, a translator, from 2A to IB.

Is that translator at
$2,100? '

Yes.
Mr. BUREAU; And the other clerks are at $2,600?
Yes.

What is the particular work that the gentlemen at $2,600 have to do that makes their salary larger than that of the translator, who is a technical man and requires special and greater knowledge than an ordinary clerk, in that he must know two languages to be able to be a translator?

The only reason I can give is that these clerks have been there a great many years, and have been advanced by the usual statutory increases until their salaries have reached this figure. The translator has been in 2A and because of the large amount of work be is called upon to do and the excellence of his work, I am advancing him from 2A to IB. In the second division, subdivision 2, there is one clerk on the list at $1,150. That is an error. There are just four altogether and the details should only be given as to four.
Taking the second division, subdivision B, I find two at $1,300, one at $1,225, one at $1,175, one at $1,150, one at $1,100. Are there any new appointments among these?

There are no new appointments except one of the messengers. When we come to the Supplementary Estimates there will be another item in the first division of subdivision B, to provide for the salary of my private secretary, which was omitted by mistake in the Main Estimates.
What is the salary?

I would like to understand what is proposed in regard to that. I see

in the Main Estimates, under Civil Government, an item:
Allowance for private secretary, $600.
I see a similar item in the estimates of all the other departments. Why is there a salary and an allowance provided? Why is it not all iput under the heading of salary instead of having one vote under the head of salary and another under the head of allowance?
That appears to have been the custom for many years in all the departments of the Government, and it has been done here the same as in other departments.

We have a new man now at the head of this department, and we might very well change 'the old order of things and not continue to put in two items, one for salary and one for allowance. Why do you not put the item in at $3,400, so that we will know what the private secretary is really getting? When you find one item here for one amount and another item some place else for another amount it looks as if you were trying to smuggle it through. Why not put it all in one sum, so that everybody will understand what the private secretaries of the ministers are getting?

I would say that this is an excellent time to change the order which has hitherto obtained. I see that the minister bows his head; but as he was for some time associated with the reform party in Ontario I imagine he might make this reform in his department with propriety.
I will take it into consideration between now and next session.

I suppose I may be allowed without being called to order, to refer to the provision made in the estimates for the minister's private secretary. In the supplementary estimates for the year ending March 31, 1919, a sum of $361 appears and in the main estimates there is another sum for this gentleman. Now T ask the minister if his private secretary is a new appointment?
Yes, a new appointment.
What position has he in the Privy Council Department?
He is my private secretary.

In the law that we have just passed we have laid it down that a private secretary shall occupy that position

only. But the minister is establishing a new rule according to the statement that he makes. This gentleman not only acts as private secretary but holds another official position in the department.

He is not performing any other duties. He is a clerk in the department; the same as any other officer, and draws the salary fixed in the Estimates the same as the private secretaries of all the other ministers.
Then he does not come under the new rule laid down in the Bill which has just been passed?
He comes under the law as it stood at the time of his appointment.

May I ask what particular duties he is performing under the law as it stands now, because after all the Civil Service Bill has not yet been assented to and has not yet the force of law. He must be holding some position beyond that of private secretary, because he is described as a clerk in the first division subdivision B. Such being the case, may I ask, what work does he perform?
He performs work as my private secretary.

The practice hitherto
has been that when a private secretary has been taken on he received an official position in the department. When the minister for whom he acted went out the private secretary reverted to that position and dropped the secretarial salary of $600 allowed to him. In this case I see that the private secretary is also a clerk in the First Division, Subdivision B although there is no work for him in the department. He was apparently appointed as private secretary to the minister and has nothing else to do; his services were not required until the minister entered the Cabinet and then only as private secretary. There is also a vote in the Estimates of $600 which brings this gentleman's salary up to $3,400. I cannot understand how that can be. If we were under the new regime as far as the appointment of private secretary is concerned I would say well and good, but the fact of putting an additional man in a certain grade, who is only required to act as private secretary to the minister, with the privilege of occupying the same clerkship after the minister retires or ceases to enjoy a seat in the 'Cabinet, when no need exists for such clerkship is not right and ought not to be entertained. I can quite understand under the old law appointing a man when a vacancy occurred to which he could

revert when the minister withdrew from the Cabinet, but I cannot understand creating a position for one for whose services there is no need except as private secretary.

Let me say to my hon.
friend that my private secretary takes the place of the Prime Minister's secretary who was in the Privy Council previously hut who now goes to another department.
Where does he go?

The Prime Minister's
secretary goes to the Department of State for External Affairs.

I understand the
private secretary was appointed by Order in Council?
Yes.

The minister says
that this gentleman is to act as private secretary. I suppose we may assume that hie duties are in connection with the business of the department?
Quite so.
He is paid a salary to act as private secretary to the minister but in connection with that hon. gentleman's public business?

Wholly in connection
with his publio business.
So it would not be part of the gentleman's work to write political literature for the Toronto Globe and other newspapers, as rumour has it he does.

That is no part of his
duties'.
And he is not paid a salary for that purpose?
Nothing whatever.

I must admit that I have read very well-written articles in the Globe under the signature of " Donald [DOT]Hunt '' and I was told that Donald Hunt was in reality the private secretary of my hon. friend. I do not know whether the report is true, perhaps the hon. gentleman can tell us as to that. I may add that the articles are very eulogistic of the hon. minister; he would blush if I were to read them to the committee to-night.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No, we want an explanation from the minister. A question has
been asked whether the private secretary to the minister is the man who writes under the pseudonym of " Donald Hunt."

I cannot furnish any information as to what my private secretary does out of office hours. He is responsible to me for the work he does in office hours. They are very lengthy hours and1 he serves very faithfully during that time. I make no inquiry as to his work outside of those hours.

That is a very nice way of shifting the question and I have been told that the hon. gentleman was rather shifty when he- was cornered. The question is a very plain one:	is " Donald
Hunt " the man who is now .secretary to the President of the Privy 'Council? That is a direct question, but I must put the question directly because I see the witness does not want to answer very readily. The committee will pardon me if the question is rather suggestive in its form.
Carried. .
No it is not carried.

I can answer my hon. friend that I am not considering, nor is my department, who are the correspondents of papers throughout the country, or who the writers for those papers are and the names under which they write, I do not think it is pertinent to the particular matter under consideration.

I think the question is pertinent and that the hon. minister is not answering it. I think we are entitled to more courtesy than the minister has vouchsafed. The question is plain and direct enough and we ought to know, when we are paying the minister's private secretary $3,400 whether he is the man who writes in the Globe or any other newspaper. The minister can answer: "I do not know whether he is the same man or not." I do not ask the hon. gentleman if he is concerned in the matter, but I ask him if his private secretary is the same man. If so, I think we have something to say about it no matter whether this gentleman writes outside of his office hours or during his office hours. I think if there is solidarity amongst the members of the Government, there is also solidarity between the minister and his private secretary. The private secretary is so close to the minister that he knows exactly what is going on. The private secretary is inspired by the minister and anything that goes out

Let me say first in reply to my hon. friend that I have never, directly or indirectly, inspired any .article that has- .appeared under the name of "Donald Hunt" or any other, with reference to the work of my department or any branch of work. I have not the least objection, if the Chairman thinks that the matter is- relevant to the item under consideration, to answer my hon. friend's question. I can say this.; so far as my secretary is concerned, never to my knowledge has he written any articles during office hours, and I know he keeps, very long office hours, often until midnight, in connection with the work of my department, the public work of the Government.
If the Chairman thinks it is a proper question, I shall be very glad to answer it.
What is that?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. minister has asked for my ruling. It is this: In voting a salary to a Government official, any member of-the House certainly has a right to ascertain what are the duties performed by that Government official. On the other hand, I do think that every hon. member of the House should accept the answer given by the minister. I understood the minister to say that he did not know what the secretary did outside of office hours, but that he had not written these articles during office hours. That answer should be considered satisfactory.
Do you hold that when a member puts a question he is entitled to an answer?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: He is entitled to such answer as any member of the Government may give.

Therefore, a member of the Opposition must stand here and be at the mercy or whim or caprice of the gentlemen who sit on the other side and have the .administration in hand. Now, I have asked the President of the Council-I will change my question. I have asked him if he knows whether this man who writes' under the name of " Donald Hunt" is the same man who is the private secretary to the hon. minister. I will ask him what is the real name of his private secretary.
My private secretary's name is Mr. Main Johnson.
Main Johnson. Has Mr. Main Johnson written in the Globe, to the knowledge of the hon. gentleman?
Order, order.

Why "Order"? I am putting a new question. The Chairman has ruled that I am entitled to an answer when I put a question. Does the hon. gentleman know that Mr. Main Johnson writes in the Globe under the name of " Donald Hunt"? If he knows it, or if he does not know it, why not say so?
I understood from the Chairman's Tuling that my answer already covered the question.
This is a new question.
Then I should say that it is a question for the Chairman to rule whether or not it is pertinent to these matters. It is for the Chairman to say.

I think that the question proposed by the hon. member for Three Rivers is a proper question, and I would suggest this: Suppose the gentleman in question, instead of writing from time to time, was turning out a series of popular novels, would it not be pertinent for this House to inquire whether it was compatible with the duty of the private secretary of a cabinet minister to spend his time also in literary effort? I think that would be a proper question. The difference between the question asked by the hon. member for Three Rivers and the 'hypothetical question put by me-is merely a question of degree. And I would humibly submit that we would like the' President of the Council, if his secretary, Mr. Main Johnson, is also this Mr. Donald Hunt, to state so frankly, and then it will be for us, if we think that there is any public interest prejudicially affected by the literary activities of Mr. Donald Hunt or Mr. Johnson to ask any other question. But before we proceed along this line it does appear to me that we are entitled to have a frank answer from the minister as to whether this literary character, " Donald Hunt," is the same gentleman who is in private life his most amiable secretary, Mr. Main Johnson.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does any other hon. gentleman wish to say anything on the point of order?
What is the point of order?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have been asked vhether the question just put by the hon.
member for Trois Rivieres (Mr. Bureau) is a proper question. I have heard the hon. member for Brome (Mr. MeMaster). Is there any other hon. gentleman desiring to say anything on the point of order?

I submit that it is none of the hon. minister's business what his private secretary does when he is not employed by the Government. He has the same right to employ his leisure time in the way he chooses, as the private seoretary of either the member for Brome or the member for Three Rivers would have. Because the private secretary of the President of the Council is employed by the Government is no reason why he is to become a serf, and must spend his leisure time in the way some member may dictate.

The hon. member for East Algorna has just said that the secretary of the President of the Council is no more responsible to this House than the private secretary to the hon. member for Brome. That cannot be taken seriously, and it is not correct. A private servant is not in any way whatsoever responsible to this House, and that would he the position of the private secretary of the hon. member for Brome. The private secretary of the President of the Council is not only the servant of that minister, but he is the servant of this House and of the Canadian people. The Canadian people are paying him. The minister himself is a public servant, and those who wait upon him in connection with the duties of his office are public servants. It is the right of every man in Canada who helps to pay the salary of a public servant to know everything about him, what he does, what he publishes. If he publishes something that we consider to be prejudicial to the interests of Canada, we have a right to know about it and to bring him to account for it. The head of any department should not stand as a shield between any officer of the department and the public. The President of the Council must answer all questions put to him with regard to his own office; he must also answer on behalf of any public servants in his employ. In a word, we have a right to know everything about the services of any man who is in the service of the country.

It appears to me that the situation is this:	the gentleman in question is employed as secretary to the President of the Council, to do certain work at certain hours an'd to the satisfaction of the minister. For that he is paid a salary out

of the public funds and for that he is accountable to the President of the Council as a minister of the Crown, and to this House. We are at liberty to question his actions in his office as much as we desire, but we do not own him body and soul. Gentlemen opposite are trying -to make a little political capital by asserting that some officials in the public service occasionally contribute to the public press, and that this gentleman is one. I am not familiar with his articles or with the trend of his writing, but I say this: as a broad principle, if we are to have first-class men in the public service, we as members' of Parliament must not act as Paul Prys in connection with the private lives of such gentlemen. We have to extend to them' broad liberties. We have to permit them to express their opinions in the public press in a free and unbiased manner. Unless we can show that they have used facts with which they have become. familiar in the discharge of their public service, we have no right whatever to raise a question as to what they do after office hours, what they write, for whom they write, how they write, or to what journals they contribute. I agree with the view expressed by the member for Algoma East {Mr. Nicholson) that it is simply not our business. It is not the business of this House to inquire into the private actions, even in connection with newspapers, of public servants. It is beneath the dignity of this House to make these investigations with the view, apparently, to attacking the President of the Council in respect of some newspaper clippings that hon. gentlemen have secured from the Toronto 'Globe or some other source. Let us get on with the business of the House and not waste time with the discussion of these trivialities.

I disagree with my hon. friend (Mr. Sheard).' The party that he follows took a very different -view only a few years ago regarding the duties of public officials. Some 25,000 men were dismissed in Canada for partisanship- turned out of office simply because they said two or three 'words in favour of the Liberal party.
Are the articles complained of partisan articles? Is this a case of partisanship? So far as I know, that has not been shown.

My hon. friend said that it made no difference what a public official did after hours; that he 
could do as he pleased. That is a new doctrine on the other side of the House.

May I ask the hon. gentle-man a question?
The 'CHAIRMAN:	The member for
Antigonish and Guystoorough (Mr. Sinclair) has the floor and is entitled to retain it unless he himself gives the member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Butts) permission to interrupt him by putting a question.
Will the member for Antigonish allow me to ask him a question?
Certainly.
' These 25,000 officials were dismissed by Blomfield Douglas under the Laurier Government-

Order. The hon.
member must not take advantage of the rules by rising to ask a question and then making a statement.
I beg your pardon, Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order.
Mt. J. H. .SINCLAIR: I was pointing out to my hon. friend (Mr. Sheard) that the doctrine that he expounded has not been accepted by the party which he now supports. On the contrary, they accept a very different doctrine; that a public official must not take part in politics; that he must not be a partisan, and that if be breaks that rule he is subject to dismissal. If that applies to ordinary officials of the Government, why should it not apply to a private secretary? If a private secretary chooses to write political articles. After hours and to take a partisan position concerning any political matter, it is open to members of the House to question his right to do so. Gentlemen on the other side must agree with this-or else the Government have entirely changed their views with regard to the matter. I repeat that that doctrine has been laid down toy the Government; that it has been held toy them; that some have suffered under it. Has this doctrine now been abolished? Has a public official now no responsibility except during office hours? If the President of the Council says that an official of the Government has the right, after office hours, to engage in any partisan activity that he wishes to engage in, of course that is a different matter; but that is not the view that has been held hitherto.

discovered that the managing editor of the Toronto Globe was receiving half his pay-

speechtext:
I do not think that would* be quite in, order. The hon. member may discuss the question after the point of order has been decided. The President of the Council was asked by the member for Trois Rivieres if his private secretary had written, certain articles in the Toronto Globe under a certain "nom de plume." The hon. minister replied that no articles had been written during office hours. The question was repeated covering generally the entire time of the said private secretary, both during and after office hours. The President of the Council required a ruling concerning the propriety of the question. I invited hon. members on both sides* for their opinions and advice upon the point of order, and they have given very much assistance to the Chair.
The hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) who is Teading the Opposition, gave it as his opinion that it was the right of any member c*f this House to probe the conduct of any official both in office hours and outside of office hours if that official did or published anything prejudicial to the interests of Canada. I took down the words at the time. The hon. gentleman went on to say that in that event it would be perfectly competent for the House to know exactly where and when such articles were written. The question of political partisanship was also introduced in the point of order. My opinion is that the conduct of any employee of the Government, in so far as his conduct outside of office hours is concerned, cannot be inquired into by a member of this House, unless, to use the words of the hon. member for iCape Breton, that employee is alleged to have done or published something prejudicial to the public interest. If that be the case, it is competent for the House to get all the details. I, therefore, rule that if the articles complained of are prejudicial to the public interest, the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) is in order. If the articles are prejudicial to the public interest the hon. member for Three Rivers should read the articles, and then ask the minister if they were written by his private secretary. Otherwise, all remarks and questions concerning the conduct of a servant of the State must be restricted *to his official conduct.

I bow, Sir, to your ruling, and I shall not take exception to it because
I do not intend to appeal. But I have another question to ask the minister. Perhaps this will throw some light on the situation. I see on page 12 of the Estimates, under second division, subdivision B, a total amount of $3,125 for 1917-18, and for 1918-19, $6,100, or almost double. Will the minister please explain the reason for that?

You told me, Sir, I might ask my question after the* point of order was settled. Might I ask this question? Your decision practically resolves itself into this, that the Parliament of Canada may pay part of the *salary of writers for the Toronto Globe. A number of years ago it was proved before the people of Canada that the editor in chief of the Toronto Globe was receiving one-half of his salary from the Peace Society of the United States which was found afterwards to b'e supported from German sources, and the other half from the Toronto Globe. I do not know whether it is now the custom of the 'Toronto Globe to have part of the salaries of its writers paid by the Government, as were formerly paid by the* pro-German United States peace societies, but whatever the facts are, we should know them.

The hon. member for
Three Rivers asked about the item being $6,100 this year as compared with $3,125 last year. The difference is this. There were two clerks in the Third Division, Subdivision A, last year, and the hon. member will notice there are none this year. The change means that those two clerks have been transferred to the other division. The clerks transferred are Mr. Miller and Mr. Olivier, who have been in the department for a very long time, and it is proposed that they be transferred from the Third to the Second Division.

On page 595 of
the unrevised Hansard appears the following question which I put to the minister:
Is Mr. Main Johnson employed in the Privy Council office or in some other Government department?
The answer was:
Yes. In the Privy Council as Private Secretary to the President of the Privy Council.
My second question was:	.
If so, was he appointed by the Civil Service Commission after competitive examination?

The answer was:
Is a graduate of University of Toronto and his appointment was made in accordance with the Civil Service Act.
There was laid on the table of the House to-day a copy of an Order in Council reading thus:
21st December, 1917.
The Board recommend that under the provisions of the War Measures Act, 1914, Mr. Main Johnson be employed as a temporary clerk In the Privy Council Office as Private Secretary to the Hon. the President of the Privy Council for a period of one year from the 12th of October, 1917, with salary at the rate of $2,800 per annum, chargeable to the War Appropriation.
God save the King.

There was another Order in Council:
The Board recommend that Mr. Main Johnson, private secretary to the Honourable the President of the Privy Council be, from the 12th of October, 1917, paid an additional allowance of $600 per annum for his services as such private secretary.
I would like to be enlightened on the subject, as the statement of the President of the Privy Council appears contradictcry to the Order in Council which I have just read.

The Order in/ Council which my hon. friend has just read is the order under which Mr. Johnson was appointed as my private secretary, but the Civil Service Act to which my hon. friend has referred makes provision for such appointment. My hon. friend will
9 p.m. have in the answer to his question the reference to the section in the Civil Service Act. The form of the order is prepared by the Clerk of the Privy Council (Mr. Boudreau), who has charge of such matters, and it has been put through in the form he suggested.
Will my hon. friend explain by what process of logic or reasoning he can join together the War Measures Act and the appointment of his private secretary?

I suppose the same reasoning as applies to the private secretaries of the other new members of the Union Government would apply to mine. The formation of the Union Government was a war measure, and in the necessary provision for the organization of the Union Government, and for the appointment of the secretaries it was proper to use the powers given by the War Measures Act.

I understood your ruling, Sir, to be that if it were shown that the articles written by " Donald Hunt," who, I presume, is admitted to be the same gentleman as Mr. Main Johnson, were prejudicial to the public interest, they would be a proper subject of inquiry by this committee. A similar matter has already come up in the British House of Commons. A member of that House, Mr. J. W. Pratt, had occupied a subordinate position-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member wishes to discuss the ruling given by the Chair he is not in order. He can only appeal from the ruling; he cannot discuss it.

I am not appealing from the ruling of the Chair; I am not discussing it; I am conforming with the ruling of the Chair. I wish to show that by British precedent, which should always be listened to in this House, articles such as this young gentleman has written are regarded in the Mother of Parliaments as prejudicial to the public interest, and this is the instance I wish to put before the committee. A certain Mr. J. W. Pratt was a member of the British House of Commons. He was also a Liberal Whip. He was a henchman and a strong party follower of Mr. Lloyd George, and he occupied part of his time in writing to the Liberal papers of Scotland letters in which Mr. As/quith was decried and Mr. Lloyd George was greatly eulogized. The matter came before the British House, where it was decided that it was an improper thing for a member of Parliament to write such letters. Now if it was an improper thing for a member of Parliament to write such letters it is a fortiori and in a greater degree, a more improper thing for the private secretary of a minister to write letters to the papers eulogizing that minister. I say that is a proper subject for inquiry by this Committee under the ruling which you, Mr. Chairman, have just given.

We are entitled to know what this gentleman does during his office hours anyway. I see by the Order in Council that this man is paid out of the War Fund, and I ask what special duties he performs for the President of the Council which have special reference to the war, outside, of course, of the great help the presence of the hon. gentleman, as President of the Privy Council, gives to the cause of winning the war by scaring the Kaiser. Is he paid out of the War Appropriation Fund for writing these articles, and will he cease writing them or did he cease writing them on the 1st of April, the date

on which the money we are asked to vote begins to apply? From that date will his war functions cease, and he become just a civil servant as private secretary to the President of the Council? We voted $500,000,000 for the War Appropriation Fund, out of which this man's salary was taken, and we are entitled to know just what special work he has performed in connection with the war, and how long he has performed it.

The salary paid to my secretary up to the first of April of the present year will be paid out of last year's War Appropriation, the payment being under the War Measures Act. The salary which will be paid during the coming year will be paid under this vote, the same as the salary of any other civil servant occupying a corresponding position.

That does not answer my question. If he was paid out of the War Appropriation he must have 'been performing some duties in connection with the war. The minister surely is not going to lay down the principle that anything at all can be charged up to the War Appropriation Fund, whether it has reference to the war or not. I do not think that is a proper principle; there are grave abjections to it. I repeat my question: What special duties was he performing in Connection with the war, to be paid out of the War Appropriation Fund?

Up to April 1 of the
present year he was performing the regular duties of private secretary to the President of the Privy Council. The matters dealt with by him are largely incidental to and out of the war. The bulk of my correspondence deal's with war matters, but I frankly say that my secretary should now be paid out of the regular appropriation of this House and that is the reason his name appears in the estimates. He is in exactly the same position as the other private secretaries who, following the formation of the Union Government, were paid out of the war appropriation, as that was the only fund available and it was the proper fund at the time the Union Government was formed.

Some time ago the President of the Privy Council notified the House that he was sending out some weekly bulletins to assist clergymen in their afternoon sermons in the rural districts. Probably this young gentleman is engaged in furnishing that data.	-
No, my private secretary is kept busy with the work of the office, and has not time to aid in the work that interests my hon. friend so much.

I had always understood that when the Estimates were under discussion the head of the department whose estimates were being considered took the opportunity to give full information to the House in regard to the work of his department. Apparently the President of the Privy Council takes the opposite course, and feels it his duty to withhold information from the House.

I think I must challenge that remark. On any matter connected with the Privy Council office on which my hon. friend desires information I shall be pleased to give it in the fullest possible way, and if any information is asked for that I have not here I shall be glad to get it.

My hon. friend may be willing to give the fullest possible information, but certainly he has not done so. Instead of showing a willingness to give information, he has shown a willingness to withhold it.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think it is quite proper for the hon. member to impute motives to another hon. member.

I was stating the fact that he had not shown a willingness to give information. The minister has said that the Union Government was formed as a war measure, and that that accounted for the Order in Council under which his private secretary was appointed and paid his salary. If it was correct for the minister to pay his private secretary as a war measure up to 1st April, he has given no sufficient reason' why he should not continue to pay him as a war measure. Is it right and proper for every member of the Government to pay his secretary and staff under the War Measures Act? If it was right then, it must be right now. Then, why ask for this vote?

We are asked to vote $44,000, and for the first time in my experience in this House we are refused information by a minister of the Crown, who hedges himself around with the rules of the House and the protection of the chairman in order not to answer pertinent questions relating to his department. Since the beginning of the session the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) has been asked question after question, has been cross-



examined and re-examined, and has always answered willingly. He had nothing to hide, and not only answered all questions that were asked, but volunteered to give further information. He said he was there to show what his department had done, and he was quite willing and glad to do it. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Crerar), the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers), and every other minister has shown the same willingness. So why should the President of the Privy Council shroud himself in silence which our questions cannot, penetrate? Is he ashamed of what is done in his department? Is he afraid to acknowledge the truth? Or what is the reason? This is the first time in-eighteen years that I have seen the House get behind the minister, -,s my hon. friend from Toronto did, who says that this is a disgrace and that we ought to go, on with something else. If there is any disgrace in this matter it is not upon our side, but it is that a minister of the Crown should hide behind the rules of the House to avoid answering a plain and courteous question. I say no minister of the Crown has a right to ask us to vote $44,000 and then dismiss our questions in a half-contemptuous manner by saying, "Oh, ask the chairman." If I ask questions about the minister's private secretary, it is because that official has been writing in the newspapers. The minister by his silence acquiesces in the statement that his private secretary was writing to the newspapers to boost him.
Are civil servants outside of office hours to be allowed to do anything they want to? We have, by his silent acquiescence, the admission of the minister that his private secretary, Main Johnson, is the Donald Hunt who is writing in the papers puffing my hon. friend. I am not willing to pass this item without registering my protest against such conduct.

I would like to know from the President of the Privy Council what the salary of Mr. Main Johnson is? I see an item in the Main Estimates:
Allowance for private secretary, $600.
*Surely that is not all the salary that Mr. Johnson receives? We would like to know what hie salary is,

If my hon. friend had
been in the House -a little earlier he would have heard the answer that I gave. In the Supplementary Estimates there is a vote for the private secretary's salary, omitted from the Main Estimates by mistake, of 
$2,800 and there is in the Main Estimates an allowance of $600, making $3,400 in all.
I would like to know how this salary compares with the salaries of other private secretaries. Is it smaller or larger than the salaries of other secretaries?

I do not know how it
compares with the salaries of other-s but it is less than he was getting before he came here.
Every one has to sacrifice something during the war.
Quite so.

Do I understand the minister to say that there are salaries larger than $3,400 per anflum paid to the private secretaries of Cabinet ministers? In what departments do the private secretaries receive more than $3,400 per annum?

I do not know but my
impression was that the Prime Minister's secretary got more than that and that the private secretaries of some other ministers got the same. I have not inquired as to what other minister's secretaries are getting.

I understand this is the first year Mr. Johnson has been employed as private secretary to a Cabinet minister. Does the minister consider that he should receive such a large salary the first year of his employment?

His work fully justifies the salary he is getting and he got more before he came here. The salary he is getting now is less than he was getting before and I consider that in the public interest his work as secretary of the President of the Privy Council is worth the payment that he is getting.

I am not conversant with the details of this writing in the Globe, but any one who takes up the papers can see that there is a puffery bureau somewhere in connection with certain gentlemen in this Government. I do not mean to say that it is a puffery bureau pnly because you can see at a glance that it is a knocking bureau as well. I would like to know if these articles are censored by the minister before they go out and if only those are allowed to go out that are puffing up the President of the Privy Council and certain other favoured ministers and gentlemen, the Chairman of the Imperial Munitions Board, for instance, and knocking certain other gentlemen.
I have never seen any such articles.

I am interested in the literary efforts of Mr. Main Johnson; in fact, we in the House all enjoy them and we should be the last people to complain of them. I always look forward to reading Mr. Johnson's prose-also his poetry. It has been the custom to give employment to literary men in the public departments of the Government. We know that in England Anthony Trollope, the great novelist, was employed in the Post Office Department. Edmund Yates was 'also in the public service in England. The late Archibald Lampman was employed in one of the departments here as a civil servant. William Wilfrid Campbell and a number of others similarly occupied positions in the public service. I might point out that the English ' gentlemen to whom I have referred were noted novelists and when we read their fiction we know that it was written with no ulterior purpose. Their works were merely imaginative, whereas the secretary of the minister, I understand, assumes to publish articles as if' they were actually truthful, and that is the difference between the English novelist and this Canadian writer.

I do not object to giving a preference to literary men in the Civil Service, as my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) suggests, but I do not think the War Measures Act should be used in that way. The hon. gentleman says that Mr. Johnson has been appointed as his private secretary. It is not only as private secretary, but he has been appointed to the Civil Service at a very large salary, and that under the War Measures Act, I believe that if the services of the gentleman were necessary to the minister for the winning of the war he ought to be paid under the War Appropriations vote and not placed over the heads of other good and faithful servants who have worked all their lives in the Privy Council office and who see this gentleman coming from Toronto and getting a large salary when their promotion is postponed because of his entry into the service. I do not think this is fair. There are many other things which have been done under the War Measures Act. My hon. friend says that Union Government is a product of the War Measures Act. Many other things are products of the War Measures Act. We all hope that peace will be restored. Then, these things will disappear, but because of the manner
144i
in which Mr. Johnson has been appointed to the Civil Service, while the war will be over, while there will be peace in the world, Mr. Main Johnson, although a product of the war, will sti'll be retained in the Civil Service and will be paid a large salary when other faithful civil servants are not getting the promotion they deserve. Certainly I think this way of using the War Measures Act, using the legislation which this Parliament enacted to promote war work, is open to strong criticism. I believe Mr. Johnson should be paid under the War Appropriation Act and not under the Civil Service Act.

Just after eight o'clock tonight a member of the Government came over to this side and suggested to us that we might get the business through fairly early and that certain resolutions would be put through so as to enable members of the Government, who wished to go, to absent themselves from the House. The President of the Privy Council has set an example of hurrying on the work by raising points of order. I would tell the minister in all frankness that he would make considerably more progress with his Estimates if he followed the example of those other members of the Government who have preceded him with their Estimates. I think the record shows that we on this side have not been unreasonable, but we are entitled to fair treatment and when a fair question is asked we are entitled to an answer.
The minister himself has acknowledged that part of his staff is paid from the War Appropriation Fund, and that raises another question. I understand that the publicity campaign throughout the country is under the charge of the President of the Privy Council. I would like to know in this connection how much money was paid for advertising the famous Order in Council, exempting farmers' sons from military service, just prior to the last general election. We are told that that Order was put through about 3rd December last and that, under the direction of the President of the Privy Council, a considerable sum of money, running from $7,000 hr $10,000, was spent. And we would like to know the exact amount so spent. The minister himself has introduced this question, and if we cannot get satisfactory information we will probe it to the bottom if it takes all night.

Might I say to my hon. friend that I have not refused to give information on any matter connected with the administration of my department. 1

shall be delighted to afford the committee the fullest possible information, at my disposal in connection with the whole of the work of that department, and if 1 have not got it here I will try and obtain it. With reference to what my hon. friend mentions, the matter came up when the War Appropriation was before the House. I speak subject to correction, because matters arose while I was away during the election campaign, but my recollection is that it was not the Order in Council to which he refers that was advertised,, 'but the judgment of Mr. Justice Duff on a test case, granting exemptions to farmers under certain conditions.
The minister .admits there was. such an Order in Council?
No, it is not part of his duties, and he has never received any such instructions.
Does the President of the Privy Council require two private secretaries to do hie work?	.
Yes. He has a secretary and an assistant secretary,. and it requires all their time to answer the correspondence that comes in, as well as to perform the necessary routine work of the office.
A double shift.
Was the assistant secretary appointed by Order in Council under the War Measures Act?

For the time being I
do not recall the form of procedure followed in connection with the appointment. I know it was made through the Civil Service Commission, and it went through the Treasury Board in the regular way, but

I do not recall the details. It is the Clerk of the Privy Council, Mr. Boudreau, who looks after these matters, and it went through in the regular way.
If 'both the minister's secretaries are employed all the time in the work of the department, how do they enjoy the opportunity to write articles and poetry for the Toronto Globe?

I think my hon. friend
could not have been listening when I told the eommittee early in the evening that no articles were written by my secretaries, or either of them, to my knowledge, during office hours for any paper.
Do they write after office hours?

The minister said a
few minutes ago that his secretaries were . kept busy from the time they went into the office until two or three o'clock the next morning.
No, I did not say that.

What time do they
have to write articles and poetry?

May I ask what is the . total amount required to be voted by this resolution? There is a vote of $54,900 and at the bottom of the page I see "printing and stationery, and sundries

the salary of Mr. Nichols?

in the War Appropriation that was voted the other day.

That has slipped
through, has it?
I want to know what "the sundries" are. There are so many things that come under that head just now that we would be interested in learning what they are.
The sundries are the same as last year, and for the same purposes.
I do not think we inquired about them last year. Anyhow, the conditions are not the same this year, and we want to know the details.

I do not think I can give my hon. friend the details now, but I shall be glad to furnish them when we take up the Supplementary Estimates. There is another item dealing with printing, stationery and all such supplies as are necessary for the carrying on of an office

such as the Privy Council Office. The money is spent under the direction of the Clerk of the Privy Council.

I would like to know if the private secretaries of the other ministers are appointed by Order in Council, or if it only happens in the case of the secretary of'the President of the Privy Council.	[DOT]
So far as I know the private secretaries of all the new ministers were appointed in that way. I know some of them were.
Then they did not have to pass a competitive examination under the Civil Service Commission?
Under the terms of the Civil Service Act private secretaries are not compelled to pass a competitive examination before the Civil Service Commission.

I asked the minister to give me an explanation of the $7,000 for sundries. His answer was-and I took it down so that there would be no misunderstanding,-that it was for printing and stationery and other expenses of the office which is under the control of the Clerk of the Privy Council. Now I ask him, in that case, why is there an item of $3,000 for printing and stationery?

I was referring generally to the item of $10,000 for contingencies. The sum of $3,000 is expressly for printing and stationery. My hon. friend is quite correct in his statement, and the sum of $7,000 'forms the balance of $10,000 for contingencies. All I can say is that it covers the usual expenses in carrying on an office of that kind. However, I shall get the details from the Clerk of the Privy Council and will give them when we take up the Supplementary Estimates.
Royal Northwest Mounted Police-salaries, $22,300 ; contingencies, $1,700.

Does this item
include the salary of the controller, Mr. McLean?
Yes.
What position does Mr. McLean occupy?
Deputy minister and controller.

Are any of the
mounted police. employed in connection with the Military Service Act?

There are some of the mounted police employed in that service in
Western Canada; some of them are assisting the Dominion police out there; and there are a few assisting the Dominion police, I think, in the province of Quebec.
Is that so?
Some five or six. They are assisting in the West.

Would the minister tell us the present strength of the force? I understand that in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan many of the services heretofore rendered by the mounted police have ceased, on the ground and for the reason that provincial constables now perform the duties undertaken by the mounted police before the erection into provinces. Many of the men, I understand, have been released. How many now remain oni the force, and what are the special duties now performed by those remaining? Are they kept near the Indian reservations?

I am very glad to answer my hon. friend. Some time after the war broke out, in view of the importance of carefully guarding the international border against possible crossing by hostile parties inspired by pro-German propaganda, and also to look after conditions in the Northwest, an arrangement was made with the Provincial Governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta whereby each of these Governments took over the work of providing their own police protection, ini order that the mounted police might be released for this special and important work of patrolling the border and of keeping in touch with all elements of the population in Western .Canada. At the same time quite a number of the force enlisted for service overseas. The number of the force, until this recent movement for enlistment as cavalry to reinforce our cavalry brigade in France, was about six hundred. The authorized strength is something over a thousand. When the request came from the overseas authorities that we should provide cavalry reinforcements for our cavalry brigade which has been operating in France, and which did such magnificent service during the great .struggle com-; mencing in March, we communicated with the Commissioner of the Mounted Police, intimating to him that this request had come for cavalry reinforcements, and the suggestion was made that if the Mounted Police cared to enlist as reinforcements for the cavalry they might go overseas at once.
As a body?
As cavalry reinforcements.
They were not to be allowed to go as a unit?

Not as a unit. It was the desire of the Police and the desire of the Government that they should go over as a unit, but the Government was not able to arrange with the overseas authorities that they should go over and go to the front as a unit. The Government did succeed in arranging that one squadron would go as a unit.
I may tell the hon. gentleman, what he probably .knows, that the Government has everything to do with sending them over as a unit, and to the front as a unit. All they want is backbone.

In that branch of the service the Minister of Militia is the one who determines, subject to the approval of the Council, what shall be done on this side, and the overseas military authorities decide what shall be done overseas. The request that came to us was for cavalry reinforcements for the existing brigade, the ranks of which had been seriously depleted in the great March offensive, and that is what was immediately required. We have succeeded, however, in getting the authorities to accept one squadron of cavalry composed of, men of the Northwest Mounted Police. The other men going over are going as cavalry reinforcements to reinforce the existing brigade in France.
Is that why Colonel Perry resigned?

He resigned because they were not authorized to go over to the front as a unit. My hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) asked the number of men in the force. We are transferring to the overseas draft 15 officers and 238 men. The Northwest Mounted Police has enlisted for cavalry recruits to go overseas 530 men, making a total of all ranks of 783 men who are now passing out of the hands of the Mounted Police to the military authorities to go overseas as cavalry reinforcements.
I am under the impression that they will pass through Ottawa, and I hope they will detrain here. If they should do so before the House prorogues hon. members will be glad to see so splendid a force as they will present. It is a fine tribute to the courage and patriotism of the men in that force that when the suggestion was made that they should enlist as cavalry recruits every ISir Sam Hughes.]	*
man in the force volunteered. Large numbers could not go because they were over age or otherwise not physically fit. That leaves on hand a force of 336 officers and men at the present time.
May I inquire if the position of controller is a new position created this year, or .an old position?
It is an old position.
Is there both a deputy minister and a controller?
That officer is the same man; he is deputy and controller.
Does this vote of $22,300 include the salaries of the 336 men?
No. This is for Civil Government; this Is the salary list of the office here. We will come to the salaries of the Mounted Police in another item:

Why should it take $22,300 for officials in Ottawa to direct 336 men who have their own officers? I know, Mr. Chairman, that the Mounted Police are very good men. There are no words of praise the minister can utter in favour of the Mounted Police that I do not at once endorse. I have had occasion to know them and meet them. It is on account of the high character of the force that it strikes me that having to pay, in addition to the salary of the minister who presides over them, $22,300 to look after 336 well trained, well disciplined, gentlemanly men, who are employed to enforce the laws of the country, is rather a large sum, especially when the officials are a couple of thousand miles away from the field of operations.
Mr. ROW'ELL: My hon. friend must bear in mind that this is the staff that has been looking after 1,200 men. We are down to 336 men at the present time simply because we. are sending overseas over 700 men.
Yet in spite of this dwindling, I notice that the appropriation is increasing instead of decreasing.
Does this item include recruiting charges?

This is simply the expense of the staff in Ottawa, and as I recollect the details the only differences are statutory increases to two or three clerks in the office.
Royal Northwest Mounted Police $1,127 -777.57.
How many members of the force are employed in connection with the Military Service Act?

Less than ten in the East,
I believe. I am not sure ol the number, because some have enlisted and are going overseas with the cavalry reinforcements. In the West I should think that the number is less than fifty, but it varies from time to time as circumstances require.
Are they paid any additional moneys on account of that service?	.
No.
I notice that there is a decrease this year in the amount to defray the expenses of pay, subsistence, billeting, forage, etc. Is the decrease in proportion per capita to the decrease in the force?

The decrease is to some extent in proportion per capita. These estimates were made on the basis of approximately GOO men,-subject to this qualification; the cost of living has so vastly increased that the cost of maintaining the Mounted Police in the West is somewhat higher than it was last year. But the main difference between the estimates of last year and those of this year is the difference in the number of men.
I assume that when these estimates were prepared it was not known that so many men were going overseas. Was this estimate made to provide for a larger number of men than are now on the force?

Yes. If the number does not increase; we shall not require the whole of this money, and it will not be spent. We shall spend only such amount as is absolut-ely required for the force engaged. When this estimate was prepared we did not know about the men going overseas.

To me it is a discovery that the Commission of Conservation has anything to do with hygienic conditions in the country, or with medical activities of any kind. There has been a public health branch of the Conservation Commission for some considerable time, and Dr. Hodge-tts, who is now in England, has been medical advisor to that branch. I know from my general knowledge of the work of the commission that they have made important investigations into questions of public health as affecting the whole country, as part of the conservation of our human resources, and they have published some reports, I believe they have looked into the question of the effect of tuberculosis op the life of the nation, the housing of the people, and the relation of housing to public health. I believe it was a result of their investigations into questions of public health that the commission decided to look into the problem of housing and town planning and brought Mr. Thomas- Adams, the town planning expert, from Great Britain to take up that question in Canada. I may say in that connection that I once heard Right Hon. John Burns- say he thought the most acute problem in Canada was the housing of our working people, and a problem to which we should devote most earnest attention if we were not to repeat the mistakes of the old land and some mistakes the cities of the United States had . made. Town planning on sound lines, he said,
was one of the urgent needs of our country. The Commission of Conservation has taken up that problem and has attempted to deal with it through the branch of which Mr. Thomas Adams- is the chief. They cannot go too far in conserving public health and doing anything that is necessary along that line for the benefit of our people. What I would object to would be the possible overlapping and want of co-operation, with resulting inefficiency and waste of public money. Otherwise, I have no objection to the expenditure of public money for the benefit of public health, and particularly for the better housing of our people.

speechtext: I apologize if I misunderstood my hon. friend.

What I did say was that if my hon. friend in charge of the department wants to figure out, as the ordinary farmer has to do, what it costs to raise a ton of hay or a bushel of potatoes on a farm, he could not stay in the business very long. However, he is able to draw on the moneys of the country and can afford to make these experiments. The idea I meant to convey was that perhaps demonstration farms would better enforce practical lessons in agriculture on the average farmer, and that if we had more of these farms all over the country where farmers could go and see what is being done and benefit by the experiments, it would be better than simply having one 'big farm at some one place.	*

The idea that my hon. friend from Cape Breton North (Mr. McKenzie) has suggested has been carried cut to a great extent in the province of Quebec during recent years. We now see along the highways in a great many parishes large placards indicating that a certain field is used as a demonstration farm by the Provincial Department of Agriculture. These demonstration farms have been of the greatest possible advantage to the farmers in the locality where they are established. Accurate records are kept showing how much it has cost to produce the crop that .is being demonstrated, and this data as well as the crop itself is open to the inspection of the farmers in the neighbourhood. This system of demonstration farms which is carried on in the province of Quebec, and which has produced

such good results, should be given earnest thought and attention by the federal authorities at Ottawa. Reference to the statistics of the province of Quebec will show the Minister of Agriculture, I think, that the wheat production in that province has made a great jump during the last three years, and the same with other crops.
I think, perhaps, that if less money were spent on the beautifying of the farm here, and a greater expenditure made on practical work in the interest of the farmers, far better results would be achieved. I hope the Minister cf Agriculture will give due consideration to the suggestion of my hon. friend from Cape Breton, and that a good many more demonstration farms will be established where the farmers can go and find out for themselves the practical results that have been obtained.	,

I spend Saturday afternoons there when the House is not sitting, and enjoy it immensely. I notice that a great many of the city people go out there and have a picnic.

Of course, it is a great convenience to the people of Ottawa to be able to get green, vegetables from the gardens, fresh bouquets' from the greenhouses, and things of that kind; I am not finding fault about that. But it would be better to have a few small experimental stations in the different localities, which could more conveniently be visited by the people. In New Brunswick there is' an experimental farm outside of Fredericton. It takes a man in my section of the province two days to get there and back. The purpose of an experimental farm is to give out practical information. I know some of the men who have charge of these farms. They are not -practical farmers and never were; they simply have the job of superintendent at a fairly good salary. When I discussed this matter last year and the year before, the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Burrell) made reference to the splendid report that he had received from the superintendent of that -experimental farm. Naturally, that gentleman would not make a report unfavourable to himself. We have deficits on these farms; we do not expect them to pay-indeed, the superintendents do not try to make them pay; they seem to think that the more money they can spend, the more -expensive horses-, harness and machinery they buy, the more the farmers will think of the experimental farm. Of course, the farmer does not know that at

the end of the year there is a deficit of anywhere from $5,000 to $50,000 in the operation of that farm. My hon. friend himself can visit these farms or send some one in whom he has confidence to inspect them and report to him as to the best method of making them really beneficial to people interested in agriculture. Has the department taken any cognizance of the fox fur farming which is one of the most important of the new industries of the twentieth century? It is second only to agriculture. 'The fur farming industry is a new departure in human industry.
In the early period of our race, when the limit of subsistence was so narrow, when our antediluvian forefathers- lived by the chase, not even communal life could exist- After a while it was discovered that they could domesticate the wild boar that they hunted, and gradually he became our modern pig. They domesticated the buffalo, she became the modern cow. They domesticated the
[fMr. Kay.]
epohiccos and he became the modern horse. They domesticated the mountain sheep and goat and gave us our modern -animals of those species. The limit of subsistence was widened so as to permit of our antediluvian forefathers forming themselves into tribes, and then internecine warfare ceased, because it was discovered they could produce better results by domestication than by hunting the wild animals. This widened the limit- of subsistence ten-fold. After a while, they discovered that the grains and the grasses on which these animals had been living could in many cases be used for human food. Then horticulture- and agriculture was born. That widened the limit of subsistence twenty-fold and enabled the generations succeeding our antediluvian forefathers to develop into nations, and so the world moved along, gradually evolving, and developing the natural resources that lay open to mankind. The solution of the problem of increased population, which always presses again-st the limit of subsistence, was found, in a measure, by the discovery of America. -Our forefathers came across here and relieved the congestion of western Europe, and what was the result? Art, science, literature, learning, civil government, -as if by magic, followed; then democracy, the thing we are fighting for to-day. After a while our own great continent was being filled up, and the people who came to -Canada moved into the United States because the climate there was warmer, living conditions were easier, and the struggle for existence was less. But before this war br-oke out the time had come when the great areas of land in the United -States were becoming filled up, and people were migrating to Canada in thousands and tens of thousands. What occurred -almost providentially, as it were, at that time? The people in my little province discovered or inaugurated, if you will, the art of furfarming. If you will follow the progress of our race and the developments that -have taken place with the widening of the limit of subsistence, yon will find that fox-fur farming is -a new cult, and one which the people of northern- climates must talke into consideration. If you will look at the map of Europe, of Asia and of North America, you will find that the bulk of the land area that is- unpeopled to-day is in this great northland. What is necessary in this- great northland is warm clothing and fuel, and- this particular industry has come into toeing from the necessities of the case, and it is up to the Department of Agriculture to take hold of it and see that

it is developed still further. If we have a paternal Government let its paternalism be practical and along the lines of development. As I said in one of my discussions before in this House, overflowing population is largely the cause of the present war, and the great territory of North America and the immense territory of Canada can only be exploited by producing conditions that will enable the northern people to grow up in this land, and it is only in the northern lands that energy is developed, because in the southern climates enervation and all that sort of thing obtains. If we are going to produce a great race in this country, we have to produce conditions that will enable our people to take up these northern lands and live in northern latitudes and so develop.
(Mr. CARVELL: Does my hon. friend think the Department of Agriculture could sell foxes for any better price than the farmers of Prince Edward Island can?

The period of frenzied finance in the fox business is past, and the business is now on a commercial basis, and.it ought never to have 'been on anything else. Originally the people who were interested in the fox business, like the people interested in western lands and British Columbia real estate, simply went after wildcats and went into a period of frenzied finance, hut that is past and it is up to the Department of Agriculture to take up this question of fur farming and develop it to the end that our great country may be populated by a strong and virile population that will dominate the world with a glorious civilization.

I
had occasion a number of years ago to go on an excursion with a lot of other farmers to an experimental farm-I was a farmer then but I am not now-and my experience with experimental farms was not very good. II am glad to hear that in some parts of the world experimental farms are a success, but the farm I visited, which was near Ottawa, was not what it should be. The potatoes were eaten up with potato bugs until there was nothing hut the stalks left, the grain was filled with weeds, and was sowed very late in the season. The cattle were extra good, and we farmers knew very well that they were fed at the Government trough; they were fed at our expense, and so it was easy to pour the feed into them. The great trouble at that farm was the patronage system. Every man about the farm, from the
labourer up, was there because of the recommendation of the member for his constituency, and that made them very independent. I am glad that in the present Minister of Agriculture we have a young man who is a capable farmer and will attend to his business. The dealer was allowed to charge five cents a bag, I believe, over and above his cost if he sold out of the car.
