Now the jobbers have been able to sell straight carloads of feed; how I do not know, because no dealer can buy a straight carload of feed from the mills. The jobbers, however seem to have been able to do it iand to. sell to the dealer. In every case they charge four or five dollars per ton more for a straight carload of bran, shorts and middlings than if a certain number of bags of flour were included. The jobber himself has charged more than the fixed price for bran and shorts, but the farmer could not complain against his local dealer, because he was in the position where he had to have the feed and. could only get a ton here and a ton there at a time, and if he complained that the dealer charged too much the dealer would give him no more feed. The live stock industry has been very, very seriously affected by the slackness or incompetence of the Canada Food Board in dealing with the question of feed stuffs. The farmer who believed the propaganda put out by the Board of Agriculture last, fall believed he would be able to buy feed at a fair price, and largely increased the number of his pigs and dairy animals generally. When winter came he found he had a great many more animals than he was accustomed to have, and more than he would have had if it had not been for this propaganda, and when he could not get the feed he required he was discouraged. His faith in

the Government and in the Department of Agriculture, to which he looks for protection, has been rudely shaken and very justifiably so. It is almost incomprehensible why the department should have allowed this situation to continue for so long as it has.
I should like to take up for a moment the question of why so, much bran and shorts and mill feed has been allowed to be exported from this country to the United States during the last year. I have tried by questions during this year to find out from the Minister of Agriculture how much bran and shorts have been exported to the United States. I asked if the exportation of bran, shorts and mill feed to the United States was allowed, and if so, how much had been exported during the last six months, and he gave me a list of a few thousand bags which had been exported ;o the West Indies and Newfoundland and never mentioned the exportation to the United States at all. I put a further question on the Order Paper asking for the exportation to the United States, and after it had been on the Order Paper for some . days it was changed to an order for a return. A day or so ago I asked the Minister of Customs when I might expect a return to that order and he professed to know nothing about it, and the Minister of Agriculture seemed to be in the same position. However, since then an hon. friend on this ride of the House has got the information, so I will not bother my hon. friend further in that respect. I find that from August, 1917, to February, 1918, [DOT]both inclusive, the value of bran, shorts and mill 'feed, exported from this country was $3,666,784, of which $3,512,945 was exported to the United States.
What is the item before the House?

Item No. 48, as follows:
For the development of the dairy industries, and the improvement of transportation, sale and trade in food and other agricultural products, $15'5,000.

It is very difficult for a farmer to understand why, when we are so short of feed in this country, this Government which had prohibited the exportation of feed without a license should have allowed such a vast amount of feed to be shipped to the United States.
What time was this feed shipped to the United States?
I will give the figures by months: August, 1917, $959,806; September, $406,091; October, $594,068; November, $806,904; December, $624,733; January, 1918, $182,563; February, $92,619.
What classes of feed were included in that?
Bran, mill feed, etc.
From what source did my hon. friend get his* information?

From the Customs Department. I will hand the statement to the minister. I do not like to take up the time of the committee-
Some hon. MEMBEES: Hear, hear.

My hon. friends are not farmers or they would be very glad to support me in a plea for better treatment of the farmer by the Government of this country. Some of our friends on the other side of the House are farmers, and some profess to be farmers, but we all know they have not stood up in the House this session for the rights of the farmers, so I am hot at all surprised to find them wearying a little because it is getting late. I think the whole question of the farming industry has received altogether too little consideration from the House during this session The agricultural industry is the backbone of the country. We have been told on the excellent authority of the Government that the farmer is doing as much to win the war as the man in the front line trenches. We have been urged to produce and still urged to produce. A great many of the ministers seem to think that all a farmer has to do is to put his seed in the ground in the spring and that the good: Lord alone will harvest it for him. Would the minister give the committee some explanation of how this feed situation has become as had as it is and some guarantee to the farmers that, during next winter at least, steps will be taken by the Government to control, not only the price of feed, hut the .millers, that flour, which is needed overseas, is not forced into the country at the expense of the farmers and that farmers will be assured a sufficient supply of feed in order' to produce the beef and pork necessary to supply our Allies? The dairy industry, unless it receives some1 convincing assurance from the Government, will be very much curtailed during next winter.

Mr. Chairman, I followed with quite a considerable degree of inter-

est the remarks of the hon. member for Miseisquoi (Mr. Kay). As far as the lack of feed for live-stock during last winter is concerned, I repeat that it was all due to the difficulty of transportation. At the time the campaign for greater hog production in Canada was embarked upon last autumn it was the intention of the Govern

ment-and the Government and the Department of Agriculture endeavoured to live up to that intention-to supply feed, or to see that feed was supplied, to the farmers who undertook the production of these, hogs. The United States last year had the largest corn crop in their history. The farmers in Indiana, Iowa, Qhio and certain other corn-producing states could not market their com throughout the winter months for the lack of transportation. I want to assure my hon. friend that the importance of the matter did not escape the attention of the department at Ottawa. Early in January I brought one of the largest cash brokers in Chicago, a man whom I know personally ias a perfectly reliable man, to discuss the whole situation with me in Ottawa and I endeavoured to make an arrangement with him whereby' corn might be purchased and *shipped into Canada at the least possible margin. The situation which resulted, in *consequence of winter storms and the desperate tie up of transportation in the United States, made it practically impossible to move the stuff. I do not think the *Department of Agriculture should be held responsible for weather conditions over which they had absolutely no control.

How was it that we could
ship so much bran to the United States if the railways were tied up?	[DOT]

I would like a closer definition of the item of " mill feed " that is at the head of the return which the hon. gentleman has handed to me. I do know that since last December the exports of bran and shorts to the United States were strictly under license from the Canada Food Board,
Not before December.
I think it was in December the licenses were first issued.
I think it was in August.

Not under the Canada Food Board. Their licenses, I think, were first issued in December. The return from which the hon. gentleman quoted was an earlier return than that which he referred
to last and which I think stated correctly the amount of bran and shorts which was permitted to leave Canada under license. However, the point is one upon which there seems to be some doubt, and I shall take means of verifying my information at the earliest possible moment, and I shall convey any information I may get to the hon. gentleman. The hon. gentleman has also complained about the difficulty the farmers had in securing bran and shorts from Canadian millers and of the prices that dealers were charging for the bran and shorts they purchased. I have just this to say, that the Canada Food Board has passed certain regulations governing the prices that shall be charged by dealers for these commodities. It is not primarily the business of the Canada Food Board to enforce these regulations. When a regulation is passed it becomes the law, and it is the. duty cf the local authorities, or any other authorities who may be charged with the enforcement of law, to see that it is carried out.
Is there still an embargo on the shipment of bran and shorts from the West eastward?

That embargo has been
removed. Reverting to the point I was discussing, if the Canada Food Board are to protect buyeTS of bran and shorts against exorbitant prices on the part of dealers, they must be supplied at least with the names of dealers who are charging these prices. IMy hon. friend made a statement that there is a reluctance on the part of farmers to supply that information for feaT that they will have difficulty in, buying from their local dealer later on. That is one of the difficulties that is inherent in the enforcement of such a law as we refer to, made and created for exceptional conditions. The position of the mills in shipping bran and shorts to customers and insisting that a flour sale shall accompany a bran and shorts sale is clearly against the regulations and instructions sent out by the Canada Food Board. I repeat that if my hon. friend Will give me the name of the mill he has made reference to, I will see that the necessary steps are taken to correct the condition of which he complains and to prevent a repetition in the future. Unless the name of the offending mill owner is given it is pretty hard to see how anything can be done. I want to assure my hon. friend that I realize-and I hope he will give me credit for my good intentions in this respect-the very great importance of seeing that those who are engaged in

our dairy industry are supplied with the feed that they require for their stock during the winter months. I hope the same conditions will not obtain next winter as did obtain during the past winter. We can reasonably expect that we shall not have [DOT]such a severe winter, and with normal transportation conditions I think there will be very little difficulty in supplying the necessary feed. If we should have another severe winter and there should be an almost complete tie-up of transportation, those are difficulties of course that are very hard to overcome.

I want to say a word or two further before the minister gets away from this item. How does he expect to answer the complaint of the hon. member for Mis-sisquoi (Mr. Kay) as regards the millers compelling any person who buys bran and shorts to take the flour also, when his own department issues different instructions prohibiting the miller 'from shipping a straight carload of bran and shorts? These are the facts. Does the minister want the evidence?
My hon. friend is surely mistaken.
I will give the minister the evidence and clear the matter up. Here is a letter from the Western Canada Flour Mills:
Of what date?
The letter is dated February 5, 1918.
I think I stated a moment ago, if I might be permitted to speak again, that these definite instructions had been sent out to the mills subsequent to that date.

Just recently, I know all about it, within the last two or three weeks after the western cattle dealers were able to send their cattle out to grass. The letter to which I have just referred contains this statement:
Re the other cars of -bran referred to we are very sorry to have to advise you that it was impossible for us to get this .past the Pood Controller in the West at the present time. He absolutely prohibits the shipment east of straight carloads of bran or shorts or even straight cars of mixed bran and shorts.
This is a statement from a reliable concern, as the minister knows well. Here is an extract from another letter dated April 23, also from the Western Canada Flour Mills:
.
As far as we can see at the present time there is no mo-re chance of this bran being shipped than there was some months ago, as no straight cars of feed are 'allowed to be shipped from any of the western mills to Eastern Canada.

It does seem to me
that the Food Control Board is making a failure in the policy of endeavouring to control prices, because as a result of that control prices' are not going down, but getting higher. In my district as a result of the attempt on the part of the Food Control Board to fix the price of bran and shorts the millers mixed eighty per cent of barley with bran, and what was supposed to cost us from $40 to $45 a ton actually cost $60 to $65. That is what they have been doing all the time, and the Food Control Board sitting in Ottawa has been issuing orders and not seeing that they are carried out.
-Mr. VIEN:	While we are considering
the development of the dairy industry, I would draw the minister's attention to the prevailing conditions in the province of Ontario and elsewhere throughout Canada in relation to the necessary help to carry on food production. The minister has probably taken cognizance of the first report of the Committee on Agriculture, in which it is stated that in the dairying counties of Ontario there is a great demand for experienced help, not only ^ in the dairying industries, but also in the farming industry generally, And the great demand for farm help exists all over the country. The chairman of the Agricultural Committee, acting upon its instructions, wired the several Ministers of Agriculture in Halifax, Fredericton, Charlottetown, Quebec, Toronto, Winnipeg, Regina, Edmonton and Victoria, asking them to inform the Committee on Agriculture by wire of the number of men and women immediately needed on farms as much for seeding as for harvesting. He has received many telegrams which are embodied in the report to which I referred, and which I may be permitted to quote.

The report in question has been placed on the table of the House, and has been dealt with by motion. Once'that is done, it is not competent for the hon. gentleman during the same session to bring forward the document and discuss it.

speechtext:
I have paid very special attention to what the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) has been saying, keeping in view the point raised by the hon. member for Simcoe. If the report had

been laid on the table of the House and disposed of, I would have had no hesitation whatever in ruling that the point of order was well taken. But I am informed by the deputy clerk that the report in question, although laid on the table of the House, has never been discussed and concurred in.

That was my opinion, and I know the facts to be as stated by the chairman. The answers to the telegrams sent out by the Chairman of the Committee on Agriculture came abundantly from all sources. From Yarmouth, N.S., under date April 29, 1918, came this telegram from Mr. Cumming:
Seeding just begun. Farmers will reduce their cultivated crops in accordance with labour shortage but for maximum production there should be at least four thousand men available.
From Fredericton, N.B., Mr. J. P. Tweed-dale wired:
New Brunswick cannot spare any man who is a farmer or farm labourer, if increased production is expeoted. With these men in the country last year hundreds of tons of hay fields, of oats and potatoes, were not harvested on account of scarcity of labour. We had farmers exerting every effort and would have splendid result. New orders re conscription farmers paralyzed the whole movement and unless positive orders issued from Ottawa insuring farmers that they will not be taken *they will not produce enough to feed city populations. Large delegation farmers here yesterday, delegation going to Ottawa.
Another telegram from Mr. Marshall, Alberta, states that if there is an average harvest between six and seven hundred men will be needed.
Another telegram came from the Deputy Minister of Agriculture of the province of Saskatchewan, which reads as follows:
Your wire re labour: demand for men well met at present but new regulations Military Service Act will take from five to seven thousand men consisting of farmers, farm labourers and farmers' sons, or from every fifteen or twenty farms in Saskatchewan, as men even approximately as useful for production are not available, the effect upon our wheat production
with seeding only about half completed can he realized.

The hon. gentleman is dealing with a report on wheat production. We are now- on a dairying item. I do not think it is competent for him to continue to discuss that matter. We are getting along late at night, and want to get away.

Before you rule, Mr. Chairman, may I be allowed to say that this report deals not only with the labour required for wheat production, -but it particularly states that in the dairying counties of Ontario there is a great demand for experienced help.
The hon. gentleman should confine his discussion to the dairying industry; he should not discuss the part of the report dealing with wheat.

The dairying industry, as much as the wheat industry, is covered in the report. Not only that, but if I may be allowed, I will say that the item under discussion reads: " For the development of the dairying industries, and the improvement of transportation, sale and trade in food and other agricultural products." And it seems that the trade in agricultural products and food will be greatly hampered if the production of food is diminished.
Mr. Chairman, this is dragging that subject in by the tail. The fact is that the report has nothing to do with that at all. The hon. gentleman has read all there is about the dairying industry.

I think the point of order raised by the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Currie) is not well taken. If you are discussing the dairy industry, surely you have a right to discuss the food given to the animals. Throughout the province of Ontario just recently we are feeding flour to our hogs. That is a fact, and I want to ask the minister this: it seems to me that this food board-
Order. The hon. gentleman knows that that is not discussing the point of order.
I beg your pardon, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The item before the Committee for discussion is, as every one will admit, a very general item, indeed. It covers the development of the dairying

industry and the improvement, transport, sale and trade in food and other agricultural products. The scope of the discussion upon such an item is necessarily very wide, and, so far, I would hesitate about' ruling that my hon. friend from Lotbiniere is out of order. I may say that he is coming perilously near the danger line, and I would ask him to assist the Committee in disposing of the item as early as possib'e by remaining well within the limits of discussion.
Mr. VIE.N: I will surely abide by your ruling, and even by your suggestion. I refer hon. gentlemen to this first report of the Select Standing Committee on Agriculture, with which hon; members generally are not familiar. I had considerable difficulty to secure a copy of it. It is not printed or distributed, but it is most interesting. You will find other telegrams than those I have already read, from Mr. Riddell, superintendent of Trades and Labour in Ontario.
I think he is in the Ontario Agriculture Department.

And another from the private secretary of the Minister of Agriculture of British Columbia. There is another from the secretary of the Department of Agriculture in Quebec. These telegrams are all to the same effect, that there is a considerable shortage of men for the farming industry all over this country. They are unanimous; these telegrams truly depict the situation at a date as late as April 29. And the Chairman of the Committee, the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders) concludes his report by saying:
The Standing Committee on Agriculture and Colonization desires to express to the Minister its opinion that his presence at its meetings would afford assistance and1 gratification to the Committee and suggests that its discussions might also be interesting and helpful to his department.
The Committee also entertains the opinion that suggestions for legislation considered worthy of the department's attention, if submitted to the Committee, would' stimulate interest in its work and offer valuable matter for assistance to the department.
And then it was moved by the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson), and seconded by the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Lang) and carried:
That it is the opinion of the Committee on Agriculture that the Minister of Militia should be requested to order (a) that actual farmers who have been called up shall be given leave of absence-

I want .to ask whether that is in order.
[The Chairman.]

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman state the point of order?
The point is that the Military Service Act has already been discussed in the House, and the hon. gentleman is starting to discuss that matter.
I am not discussing that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Has the hon. member for Lotbiniere anything to say on the point of order?
Nothing, Mr. Chairman, except that I am concluding the report before I come to the discussion of the item now under consideration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: In connection with the point of order just raised by the hon. member for North Simcoe, I beg to say that I will permit the reading of the report passed by the Committee on Agriculture and which has not yet been concurred in by the House. I may add that any discussion which might possibly arise out of that report relating to the Military Service Act or the Order in Council concerning the Military Service Act, I would consider to be absolutely out of order.

The concluding recommendation in the report is:
That no actual farmers be required to report until all others in the class affected by the Order in Council of 20th April, 191S, have been .put in service; such leave of absence and d*lay in reporting to be conditional upon their actual employment in farming.
I think, 'Sir, that another very important document was sent to the Government at a very late date, as late as last week, in which the conference of farmers, recently held in Ottawa, embodied its views. I understand that they have sent that report to His Excellency the Governor General and that it has been referred by him to the Privy Council.
What steps has the department taken with a view to securing for the farming industry the men who are so badly needed? The evidence of this need was given by these gentlemen who met in conference from all parts of Canada, and is set forth also in the document to which I refer, of which my hon. friend must surely have a copy. The Prime Minister told us the other day that the document was on its. way and that he expected it to- reach his office shortly.

There was a sufficient supply of farm help to attend to the seeding operations; at least, the reports show that that was the case in Western Canada. Any
disturbance of farming operations result-

ing from the recent amendments to the Military Service Act "will have to be looked after in the most effective way that can be devised. The registration that is to be made by the Canada Registration Board will afford a great deal of useful information in working this problem out.

Has'my hon. friend taken cognizance of the conclusions arrived at by the last conference of farmers held in Ottawa, as embodied in the report to which I referred a moment ago? Has any action since been taken?
The time intervening has been short. My hon. friend scarcely expects that a policy could be mapped out in so short a time.
Then my hon. friend has received the document of which I speak? He intimates that he has taken cognizance of it.
I have not received it, but I was present and heard the representations made by the delegation of farmers which was here last week.
Has my hon. friend taken any steps to carry out or give effect to the conclusions embodied in the first report of the standing committee on agriculture?
Any announcement in that respect would be made by the Prime Minister.
Is the Government really considering the matter?

What is the policy of the Government with reference to the farming interests concerned? Has the Government modified its views respecting the enforcement of the recent Order in Council calling even the farmers to military service?
My hon. friend can hardly expect me to answer that question. Any announcement of policy would of necessity come from the Prime Minister.

The Food Control Board passed an order early in the winter fixing the price of bran and shorts and leading the farmers to believe that they or the Government were going to prevent the millers from profiteering. The millers were allowed a profit of twenty-five cents a barrel on flour and were to sell bran and shorts practically at cost. It has been brought to the attention of the department that the millers are mixing bran and shorts with barley and selling the product at $65 a ton. That should be stopped, because they are
making a greater profit now than they did before the price was fixed. Another thing. The farmers' clubs were buying carloads p.f bran, and shorts and they were compelled to take a certain percentage of flour, in each car. I have it on good authority that in some districts the farmers actually fed that flour to their hogs; they had more than they wanted. Now, another order has been issued, providing that if a farmer who lives within five miles of a village has more than 6ix weeks' supply of flour in store, he must take the surplus to the man from whom he bought it. In order to get the bran or feed, these farmers' clubs were obliged to buy more flour than they wanted and now they have it on their hands. Whom are they to- send it back to? ,

It is true that an order did issue from the Food Board a few weeks ago requiring those who had certain supplies of flour to return the surplus to dealers from whom they had purchased it. Undoubtedly that order worked a hardship on the farmers. The matter was drawn to the attention of the Food Board and and amending order has been or will be sent out in the immediate future requiring that farmers shall simply report to the dealers the stocks of flour that they have on hand. (The end in view, of course, is' to gather up as much flour as possible for shipment overseas to- meet the pressing need there until the new wheat crop goes on the market. As to the feeding of flour to the hogs, there is this peculiar position: flour, bran and shorts mixed together was the cheapest food that a farmer could feed his hogs, owing to the price of barley and oats The price of wheat was- fixed by the Board of Grain Supervisors last fall on the basis of $2.21, Fort William, while the price of oats and barley was not fixed. It was urged' on the' board that the price of oats should also be fixed, but it was rather difficult for Canada to take action in that respect unless similar action was taken by the United States. AlthougTi in some cases flour has been fed to the hogs, I think the practice has been by no means widespread.
The reason why the price of oats went above the price of flour and wheat was because of the demand for seed*.	.
The minister asks me to give him the names of some millers who were forcing flour out with their cars. I name two: the Lake of the Woods Milling Company, and the Ogilvie Milling Company.

Can we expect very shortly *a definition of the Government's policy as to the supply of men for the farming industry? The minister stated that he could not tell us what change would take place or if any change would take place.
Mr. CER'ERAR: I would suggest that the hon. member direct his question to the Prime Minister at the morning sitting.
Suppose we take the case of a farmer who is the owner of a butter factory and who is making butter and cheese. This man is of military age-

On motion of Hon. A. K. MACLEAN (Acting Minister of Finance), the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to provide that the provisions of The Zinc Bounties Act, 1916, chapter twenty-seven of the Statutes of 1916, [DOT]be renewed and continued in force until the thirty-first day of July, 1920.
Will the minister explain the resolution?

Under an Act of Parliament passed in 1916, it was provided that a bounty of two cents a pound be paid upon zinc produced in Canada, when the price fell below the standard price of zinc on the London market, which is the world market for that product. It was, however, provided in that Act that no bounty should be paid during the war, and that the amount, when payable, should not exceed 1400,000. In 1915, after the beginning of the war, it was considered very desirable in the ' national interest that Canada
1 a.m. produce a high-grade zinc. It was at that time not produced in Canada, and I hardly think in the United States, and it -was particularly desirable for use in munition works. The Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of British Columbia was induced by the Shell Committee, and later on by the Imperial Munitions Board, to incur very heavy expenditures on capital account in erecting a plant to produce this high-grade zinc, and altogether they spent $2,500,000. It was represented t-o them that they would receive from the British Government and from some of the other Allied powers orders continuously during the war, so as to enable them to amortize the expenditures they had made in erecting their plant in order to produce this high-grade zinc. They did produce a very considerable quantity, about 30,000 tons altogether, for which they received 15 cents per pound. The price *previous to that, in the earlier part of the war, was 40 cents per pound, and Canada and Great Britain have had the advantage of that reduced price brought about by the entrance of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company into the market. By reason of Russia's withdrawal from the war and by reason of the entry of the United

States into the war, all orders for high-grade zinc will cease on the 30th day of June in .this year.
When the Consolidated Smelting Company embarked upon the enterprise of producing high-grade zinc, the Government of the day recognized it was in the national interest to pay a bounty under certain conditions, and now that the company is unable to sell its product to any of the countries of the world now engaged in the war, they claim that this assistance should be rendered to them now and for two years to come. The total amount to he paid as bounties will not exceed $400,000, the amount stated in the Bill. Seventy-five per cent of the zinc consumed in Canada is what is known as low-grade zinc; that is not the technical term, but the metal is low grade. It is, however, just as useful to the greater (part of the trade as the high-grade zinc, and generally sells at seven cents per pound. The Consolidated Mining & Smelting Company anticipate that gradually they will be able to reduce their costs of the high-grade ore from 9 cents, which is the cost at the present time, to 7 cents. If they reduce it to 8 cents we shall only have a bounty of one cent a pound to pay, representing the difference between the present London standard price and the price they get on this side of the water. The main purpose of the resolution and of the Bill will be to accelerate the time within which they shall receive payment of this bounty. Upon the second reading of the Bill I shall be pleased to give any further information that is desired.
What has been paid already?
Nothing whatever.
There is no enlargement of the original appropriation?
No.
Is it the high-grade or the low-grade zinc that costs 9 cents a pound?

The high-grade zinc that is now produced electrolitically by the Consolidated Mining & Smelting Company. They have been able, by the erection of a modern system of production, to reduce their costs from 40 cents to 9 cents.
How is it that if it costs 9 cents a pound to produce, it sells for 7 cents a pound?

That is the low-grade metal, which is produced much more
cheaply and which is not so desirable for munitions purposes
The higher grade zinc must sell for a higher price.
There is no market for it at the present time except the Canadian market, and the Canadian market largely consumes the low-grade metal.
Could we not sell it to the United States?

There is no demand for it in the United States as they are producing the ore in very large quantities themselves, and largely by virtue of the financial credits being given by Great Britain to the United States, Great Britain is obtaining her requirements from the United States. It was expected that large contracts would be received from Russia, but now that she has withdrawn from the war the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company do not anticipate any further trade with her.

A further study of the subject may change my opinion, but it appears to me that if there is such a small market for this product it is scarcely a commendable policy to spend $409,000 to encourage such an industry. We might sipend the money on something more productive.

My hon. friend must remember that it was of vital importance to national interests at the time this industry was started to produce a high-grade zinc in Canada. The industry was started on the request in the first instance of the Shell Committee, and upon request later made by the British Government. It was then the Canadian Government intervened,, and sought to extend aid to the company in producing this high-grade zinc. Subsequently an Act of Parliament was passed providing for this assistance, so we are almost in honour bound to stand by the contract made with this company. The maximum to be paid will ibe $400,000, but I hope the amount will not meet that figure.

I understand the
promoters of this Bill are monopolists, and while I am not going to oppose this measure to-night I give notice to the minister that when the Bill comes up for second reading we shall have to investigate. I understand that the ordinary mine owners of British

Columbia, while they may not be opposed to this and probably will benefit by it to a certain extent, want other considerations besides a bounty on zinc and lead. I would draw the minister's attention to the fact that the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company and the Trail Smelter are practically one and the same thing and that the Consolidated produces practically all the ore in the East Kootenay district. The yearly figures are as follows: Paradise, 1,089 tons; Sulliv.an (zinc), (this is the Consolidated), 30,579 tons; Daly Burton, 34 tons; Hidden Treasure, 2 tons; St. Eugene, 267 tons; Providence, 30 tons; Sullivan, 229 tons; St. Eugene, 214 tons. So the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company practically own the whole shooting match as far as East Kootenay is concerned, and you might say the same thing of the whole mining industry of British 'Columbia with the exception of Rossland. The Miners' Association have been asking the Government for a duty of five per cent on zinc and lead coming in from the United States, and also for a Royal Commission to investigate the whole question of the Trail Smelter and the mining industries of that section of British Columbia. I would ask the minister to consult with his colleagues and see if he cannot agree when the Bill comes up for second reading to give the ordinary miners, the proletariat, a Royal 'Commission to investigate this whole question to find out whether it is not one giant monopoly which is sucking the blood of the common people of British 'Columbia. Unfortunately, the people of British Columbia are not represented to-day in this House by a single Liberal member, and they take their political life in their hands to go against this hydra-headed monster of monopoly.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.
Mr. A. K. MACLEAN thereupon moved to introduce Bill No. 109, to provide for the payment of bounties on zinc produced and zinc ores mined in Canada.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

subtopic: RETIREMENT OF AGED AND INFIRM CIVIL SERVANTS.

speechtext:
House in Committee on the following proposed resolution.
That it is expedient to provide that the Civil Service Commission shall forthwith prepare and submit to the Governor in Council for approval the names of all officers, clerks and employees 
who, owing to advanced age, failing health, or lack of experience or ability, or other cause, are not capable of rendering or do not render efficient service to the State, and should, therefore, be retired from the public service; stating the conditions under which each such officer, clerk or employee should be retired, including the pecuniary provision, if any, that should, in the opinion of (the Commission, be made for any such officer, clerk or employee, and in each case the date recommenced for his retirement; and for the pecuniary provision to be made for any such officer, clerk or (employee, and for the determination of the amount to be paid, the deductions therefrom and the method by which the amount of such deductions shall be paid; and that upon approval by the Governor in Council of the recommendations of the Commission, such officer, clerk or employee shall be retired upon the date fixed and conditions specified, and any moneys required for such pecuniary provisions may be paid out of any unappropriated moneys in the Consolidated Revenue Fund of 'Canada.-'Hon. A. K. Maclean, Mr. Boivin in the chair.
Hon.. Mr. FIELDING: It is too late to die-cuss the resolution, but when it comes up at a later time I would be glad if the minister would give us some further information. I do not know whether ot not the House realizes that under this resolution we will 'be establishing a superannuation system. Years ago, not very wisely-I think it was one of the mistakes of our own Government-the superannuation system was practically abolished. Here we aTe going to re-establish it, not by a direct Act of Parliament, but we are going to leave it to the Governor in Council. The reasons may be very strong, and I am not opposing it, but I am only asking the House to consider what it means', because Parliament ought to have a clear 'conception of the very large order which the Government" is receiving in this form.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.
Hon. A. K. MAOLEAN moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 110, respecting Aged and Infirm members of the public service.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
